rows: base-term-beginner
Beginner (novice)
A lifter who still progresses on a simple, repeated routine. The 2009 ACSM position stand uses novice for people with no lifting experience, or none for several years.
base-same-start-any-goal
A first programme looks much the same whatever the long-term goal
Health, physique, sport and powerlifting beginners need the same base first. The goal starts to shape the plan at the intermediate stage.
base-least-training-that-works
Start with the least training that still makes you progress
If a small amount of training produces gains, extra work adds risk and uses up the room you will need later.
base-mistake-years-in-gym
Counting years in the gym as proof you are past the beginner stage
Time served does not make a lifter intermediate. Stable technique, the ability to work hard and measurable gains do.
base-when-beginner-ends
You stop being a beginner when simple training stops producing gains
Expect roughly 6 to 12 months of proper training before a beginner routine runs out, by McDonald's estimate.
base-num-beginner-months
Time before a beginner routine runs out
McDonald's estimate of when a beginner becomes an intermediate. The 2009 ACSM stand puts intermediates at about 6 months of consistent training.
6-12 months of proper training
base-tendons-adapt-slowly
Tendons adapt more slowly than strength rises
Strength can climb by almost a third in two months while tendon stiffness has not yet changed, so add load more slowly than strength allows.
base-term-work-capacity
Work capacity
The amount of training you can do and recover from. Beginners build it slowly. Leaving every session exhausted means the workload is ahead of it.
base-effort-is-learned
The ability to work hard is learned in small steps
New lifters stop long before real fatigue. Pushing a little past the point where you would normally stop resets that limit over time.
base-checklist-outgrown-beginner
Signs you have outgrown a beginner programme
Drawn from Lyle McDonald's criteria. Most of each group should be true before you change to an intermediate plan.
base-term-training-variables
Training variables (loading parameters)
The settings that define a programme: intensity (how heavy), volume (how many sets and reps), frequency (how often) and exercise choice. Rest between sets and speed of movement are often added.
base-beginner-load
Beginners gain strength on loads as light as 60% of their max
Untrained people gained the most strength at about 60% of one-rep max in a large meta-analysis, so there is no need to start heavy.
base-num-beginner-load
Load that maximised strength gains in untrained people
Mean training load with the largest strength effect in untrained people across 140 studies. Trained people needed 80%.
60 % of 1RM
base-beginner-sets
One set per exercise is enough to start; build to two or three
A single set gives a new lifter most of the early strength gain. Extra sets add practice and a little more, at the cost of time.
base-beginner-reps
Sets of 8 to 12 suit most beginners; sets of 5 need restraint
Moderate reps keep the weight modest and give plenty of practice. Low reps work when someone stops you loading the bar too fast.
base-beginner-frequency
Train the whole body two or three times a week at first
Three weekly sessions gave untrained people the largest strength gains in one meta-analysis. Two is close and easier to schedule.
base-num-two-vs-three
Share of the three-day result from two sessions a week
McDonald's estimate for beginners training twice a week instead of three times. A coaching figure, not a pooled result.
about 80 % of the strength gain
base-mistake-beginner-split
Starting on a one-muscle-a-day bodybuilding split
A split trains each exercise about once a week, which starves a beginner of practice and invites far more sets than needed.
base-table-beginner-by-goal
How a beginner plan shifts with the long-term goal
The base is shared. These are the adjustments Lyle McDonald describes for each aim, arranged here as a comparison.
base-free-weights-vs-machines
Free weights and machines build similar strength and size
A meta-analysis found no difference in muscle growth, and strength rose most on whichever equipment people had trained with.
base-table-free-weights-machines
Free weights and machines: the practical differences
Results are similar, so the choice turns on practical points. These are the ones McDonald weighs for a new lifter.
base-term-compound-isolation
Compound and isolation exercises

A compound (multi-joint) exercise moves two or more joints and works several muscles, as in a squat or row. An isolation (single-joint) exercise moves one joint, as in a leg extension or curl. Both exist as free-weight and machine versions.
base-compound-and-isolation
Multi-joint lifts save time; single-joint lifts fill the gaps
With total work matched, multi-joint training gave larger strength gains than single-joint training and the same change in body composition.
base-machine-circuit-start
A machine circuit is a sound first programme
For an untrained adult who wants general fitness, simple machines taught over a few sessions do the job with little to learn.
base-keep-exercises-first-weeks
Keep the same exercises for the first six to eight weeks
A new movement needs weeks of practice before you can load it or judge it, so early variety slows learning.
base-starting-weight
Find first weights by starting with the lightest option available
Begin with the empty bar, the empty sled or the first plate on the stack, and add weight in later sets or sessions.
base-mistake-bodyweight-formula
Setting first weights from a body-weight formula
Rules that tell a beginner to squat or press a fixed share of body weight fit some people and badly overload others.
base-rep-range-progression
Use a rep range and add weight when you reach the top of it
Work in a range such as 8 to 12. When the top number arrives in good form, add a little weight and build the reps back up.
base-num-load-increase
Load increase once you beat the rep target
The 2009 ACSM stand's step size, applied when you can do one to two reps more than the target number.
2-10 % of the current load
base-jumps-as-percentage
Judge a weight jump as a percentage of what is on the bar
The same plate is a small step on a heavy lift and a huge one on a light lift, which hits smaller lifters and small exercises hardest.
base-mistake-weight-every-session
Adding weight every session whether or not the last one was clean
Plans that ask for more weight each time work when a coach makes the call. Alone, lifters keep adding after technique has begun to slip.
base-term-back-cycle
Back-cycle (reset)
A planned step back after a stall: cut the load by 10 to 20%, then build up again over three to four weeks and aim to pass the old best.
base-stall-and-back-cycle
After two weeks without progress, drop the load and build back up
A stall means about two full weeks with no gain in weight or reps. The standard answer is a 10 to 20% step back and a steady rebuild.
base-num-back-cycle
Step back after a stall
The reset McDonald describes after two weeks without progress, followed by a rebuild over three to four weeks.
10-20 % off the stalled load
base-after-beginner
The usual next step is more sets, spread over upper and lower days
When simple training stops working, most lifters need more weekly work, and splitting the body in two keeps sessions a sensible length.
base-term-double-progression
Double progression

A way of progressing inside a rep range such as 6 to 12: add reps from session to session until you reach the top of the range, then add weight, which drops you back toward the bottom, and build up again.
base-term-maximal-strength
Maximal strength

The greatest force you can produce in one effort with no time limit. In the gym it is measured as a one-rep max. Coaches outside the lifting sports often track a 3- or 5-rep max to avoid true maximum attempts.
base-term-relative-strength
Relative strength
Strength divided by body weight. It matters most where you move your own body or compete in a weight class. Gaining weight faster than strength lowers it.
base-strength-size-neural
Strength is muscle size multiplied by how well the nervous system uses it
Bigger muscle raises the ceiling for strength. Skill, coordination and leverage decide how much of that ceiling you reach.
base-strength-zone
Maximal strength work means heavy loads, few reps and long rests
The 2026 ACSM stand found strength was enhanced by loads of 80% of max or more. Convention puts dedicated strength work at 85% and up for 1 to 5 reps.
base-table-strength-dose-by-status
Dose that maximised strength gains, by training status
Mean values from two meta-analyses and the 2026 ACSM overview. The older analyses counted sets that were mostly taken near a repetition maximum.
base-who-needs-max-strength
Not everyone needs true maximal strength training
Lifting sports and weight-class athletes need it most. For physique goals it is occasional, and for general health sets of 5 to 8 are heavy enough.
base-strength-base-for-sport
For most sports, strength is a base to build and then maintain
Stronger athletes sprint, jump and change direction better, but most sport actions last 0.1 to 0.2 seconds, too short to use maximal strength.
base-grinding-cost
Grinding lifts cost more recovery than lifts that are made or missed quickly
A rep fought through for several seconds taxes muscle, joints and nervous system far more than a fast lift, which limits how often it can be done.
base-term-prilepin
Prilepin's chart

A table from Soviet weightlifting, attributed to A. S. Prilepin, that gives reps per set and total reps in a session for each band of intensity. It records what elite weightlifters did and was never tested in an experiment.
base-prilepin-limits
Prilepin's chart describes elite weightlifters, so its upper volumes are too high for most
The chart's logic is sound: keep reps per set well under the most you could do, and cut total reps as the load rises. Its numbers come from a narrow group.
base-num-strength-reps-per-session
Heavy reps per exercise in a strength session
From the old rule of 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 5 reps, which McDonald endorses for strength work. Stay low nearer 90% of max, higher nearer 85%.
9-25 reps per exercise
base-mistake-heavy-everything
Programming five heavy sets of five on every exercise
Heavy low-rep sets need rests of several minutes, so more than one or two such lifts makes a session unworkably long.
base-term-power
Power (muscular power)
Work divided by the time taken to do it, or force multiplied by speed. Lifting the same weight through the same distance in half the time doubles the power.
base-term-rfd
Rate of force development (RFD)
How quickly force rises at the start of an effort. Sprint steps, jumps and throws allow only about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds, so the force you can reach in that window matters more than your slow maximum.
base-term-force-velocity
Force-velocity curve
The trade-off between the force a muscle can produce and its shortening speed: the faster the movement, the lower the force. Power, the product of the two, peaks in the middle of the curve.
base-table-force-velocity-bands
Kinds of training along the force-velocity curve
From heavy and slow to light and fast. Loads are from the cited reviews; the sorting of sports follows Lyle McDonald's discussion.
base-table-peak-power-load
Load that gave the highest power output, by exercise
From two meta-analyses that sorted loads into three zones. The best load for power differs between exercises, so one percentage does not fit all.
base-ordinary-lifts-poor-power
Ordinary lifts make poor power exercises because the bar has to be slowed
A squat or bench press starts and ends at rest, so part of every fast rep is spent braking. Throws, jumps and Olympic lifts let you accelerate to the end.
base-olympic-lifts-for-power
Olympic lifts build power only once they can be done well with real loads
The lifts are fast by nature and produce very high power, but they take a long time to learn. Short on time, use simpler explosive exercises.
base-mistake-power-when-tired
Carrying on with jumps, throws or fast lifts after the snap has gone
Power work only trains power while each rep is near your best. Slower reps add fatigue and nothing else.
base-num-power-set-length
Longest useful all-out power set
McDonald's limit for holding maximal power, after which output falls. He pairs sets this short with rests of 3 minutes or more.
6-8 seconds
base-power-simple-measures
Use a mark, a tape or a stopwatch to judge power work
A target to reach on every rep shows when a set should end and whether you are improving, with no electronics.
base-fast-lift-load-rule
For fast lifting on ordinary exercises, take 20 to 30% off your working weight
A lifter who normally works at 80 to 85% of max lands at about 50 to 65% this way, inside the range where squats and bench presses produce most power.
base-num-fast-lift-drop
Reduction from working weight for fast, explosive sets
McDonald's shortcut for lifters who train at about 80 to 85% of max. It gives roughly 50 to 65% of max, within the power range.
20-30 % off the working weight
base-intent-to-move-fast
Try to move a heavy bar fast even when it moves slowly
In a 16-week trial, trying to move explosively produced the same high-speed adaptations whether or not the limb moved.
base-mistake-squat-before-jumps-rule
Holding off all jumping until you can squat twice your body weight
The old rule was written for depth jumps, the hardest plyometric drill. Easy hops, jumps and throws need no strength threshold.
base-session-order
Order a session from fast and skilled work to slow and fatiguing work
Speed, skill and power suffer most from fatigue, so they come first. Heavy strength follows, then higher-rep work, then conditioning.
base-term-pap
Post-activation potentiation and complex training

A short rise in explosive performance after a few heavy efforts. Complex training alternates heavy sets with jumps to use it. A meta-analysis of 47 studies found small to moderate effects, larger in stronger, more experienced lifters.
base-power-progression
Power work is progressed slowly, by output more than by load
Throwing further and jumping higher at the same load is the progress. Added weight changes these exercises more than it seems.
base-stop-after-personal-best
After a true maximal personal best, end that work for the day
A new best on an all-out lift or sprint is a stress the body has not met before. Stacking more on top can cost weeks.
base-term-metabolic-training
Metabolic (depletion) training
Weight training with light loads, sets of 15 to 20 or more and rests of a minute or less. It empties muscle glycogen and builds tolerance for fatigue more than it builds size or strength.
base-metabolic-training-uses
High-rep, short-rest training builds fatigue tolerance more than size or strength
Light loads, 15 to 20 reps and rests under a minute suit muscular endurance and work capacity. McDonald rates them a poor main method for growth.
base-mistake-high-reps-to-cut
Switching to light weights and high reps to get lean
High-rep circuits burn energy but hold muscle and strength poorly, and holding muscle is the main job of lifting during a diet.
base-mistake-high-rep-barbell-circuits
Building high-rep circuits around technical barbell lifts
Under heavy fatigue, squat technique changes within the session. Simple exercises are the safer choice for high-rep, short-rest work.
base-term-hypertrophy-hyperplasia
Hypertrophy and hyperplasia

Hypertrophy is the enlargement of existing muscle fibres. Hyperplasia would be a rise in the number of fibres. Growth from training in humans is explained by hypertrophy; hyperplasia is unproven and, in McDonald's view, minor at most.
base-term-myofibrillar-sarcoplasmic
Myofibrillar and sarcoplasmic hypertrophy
Myofibrillar growth adds contractile protein, the part of a fibre that produces force. Sarcoplasmic growth is a disproportionate expansion of the fluid and stored material around it.
base-sarcoplasmic-evidence
Every training style builds both contractile protein and muscle volume
Some evidence shows the fluid part of a fibre can expand faster than its contractile protein, but no method produces one kind of growth alone.
base-tension-primary
Mechanical tension is the main growth signal; damage and burn are secondary
Reviews rank mechanical signals as the prime trigger for hypertrophy. Muscle damage is probably not needed, and metabolic stress looks minor.
base-hormone-spike
The hormone rise after a session does not decide how much you grow
In 49 trained men, the post-exercise rise in hormones was unrelated to gains in muscle or strength over 12 weeks.
base-num-reps-per-session
McDonald's growth guideline for reps in a session
His working range at about 60 to 85% of max, citing a 2007 review he reads as favouring 30 to 60. Newer analyses count weekly sets.
40-70 reps per muscle a session
base-indirect-volume
Muscles already worked by compound lifts need about half the direct work
After pressing or rowing, the arms and rear shoulders have done part of their work. McDonald halves their direct volume.
base-match-exercise-to-reps
Match the exercise to the rep range
Heavy sets of 5 to 8 suit compound lifts. Sets of 12 to 20 suit exercises with no weak link and little danger if form slips.
base-mistake-redundant-exercises
Doing three or four near-identical exercises for one muscle
Barbell, dumbbell and machine versions of the same press train a muscle the same way. The extra exercises only add sets.
base-programmes-share-core
Growth programmes that last share the same few ingredients
Plans that look very different on paper all combine progressive loading, some fatigue work, moderate volume and regular easier weeks.
base-mistake-8-12-only
Treating 8 to 12 reps as the only range that builds muscle
Growth has been shown across a wide span of loads. The 8 to 12 range is a convenient middle, not a boundary.
base-term-rep-continuum
Repetition continuum
The idea that low, moderate and high reps lean toward strength, size and endurance in turn. The zones overlap: the heavy end of size training is the light end of strength training.
base-term-volume-load
Volume load (tonnage)
Sets multiplied by reps multiplied by the weight lifted, added up over a session or a week. Three sets of 5 with 100 kg (220 lb) is 1,500 kg (3,300 lb).
base-table-counting-volume
Three ways to count training volume
Each count answers a different question and each can mislead. The comparison follows Lyle McDonald's discussion of volume.
base-term-technical-failure
Technical failure
The point in a set where good form can no longer be kept, even if a rougher rep is still possible. On skilled lifts it comes before momentary muscular failure and is the safer place to stop.
base-rep-out-test
Use an occasional all-out last set to check your working weight
Every three or four weeks, push the last set as far as it will go. Far more reps than the target means the weight is too light.
base-table-training-types
Four kinds of weight training and the loading that defines each
Loads, reps and rests from the 2009 and 2026 ACSM position stands. The zones overlap, and most programmes use more than one.
base-term-intensity-load-effort
Load intensity and effort intensity
Two different meanings of intensity. Intensity of load is the weight as a share of your one-rep max. Intensity of effort is how close the set comes to failure, often given as RPE or reps in reserve.
base-term-rm-load
Repetition maximum (RM) load
The top weight a lifter can manage for a stated number of reps in good form. A 10RM is a load you can lift ten times and not eleven. A zone such as 8 to 12RM sets the load without a percentage.
base-intensity-two-numbers
Describe a set with two numbers: how heavy and how hard
The same weight can be an easy set or an all-out one. Load says how heavy the bar is; effort says how near failure the set went.
base-rm-zone-not-percent
Outside the lifting sports, set loads by a rep-max zone, not a percentage
A percentage needs a tested max and assumes everyone gets the same reps at it. A rep zone with a few reps in reserve needs neither.
base-warm-up-for-fast-work
All-out fast work needs a longer warm-up than its light loads suggest
A sprint, jump or throw is a maximal effort even with no load, so the warm-up should build to full speed in steps.
base-term-general-specific-warm-up
General and specific warm-up

A general warm-up is light whole-body activity that raises body temperature. A specific warm-up is progressively heavier sets of the exercise you are about to train, which also rehearse technique and ready the nervous system.
base-general-warm-up-light-sweat
End the general warm-up at a light sweat
Five to ten minutes of easy activity is typical. The endpoint is feeling warm, and many lifters can use light first sets instead.
base-table-warm-up-sets
How many warm-up sets, by situation
Lyle McDonald's guidance gathered into one comparison. Heavier loads, more technical lifts and stronger lifters need more sets.
base-num-warm-up-sets-heavy
Warm-up sets before heavy triples
McDonald's guide for work at about 85 to 90% of max. Sets of 12 at moderate loads need only one or two.
4-7 sets
base-mistake-warm-up-sets-too-hard
Taking warm-up sets close to failure
High-rep sets on the way up tire you before the sets that count. Keep warm-up sets short and cut the reps as the weight rises.
base-warm-up-set-feel
End a warm-up set at the rep where the weight starts to feel easy
Reps in a warm-up set often feel stiff, then suddenly smooth. That change is a better stopping point than a fixed count.
base-stretch-before-lifting
Stretch before lifting where tightness blocks a safe position
Static holds up to 30 to 45 seconds did not reduce maximal muscle performance in a review of 106 studies. Longer holds did, when tested straight afterwards.
base-term-dynamic-stretching
Static, dynamic and ballistic stretching

Static stretching holds a muscle at length without moving. Dynamic stretching moves a joint under control through a range that grows with each rep. Ballistic stretching flings the limb through the range and has fallen out of favour.
base-foam-rolling-optional
Foam rolling before lifting is optional and does not replace warming up
Rolling before exercise gave a small gain in flexibility and a negligible change in strength in a meta-analysis of 21 studies.
base-warm-up-heavy-single
A single at the working weight is an optional primer for experienced lifters
Some lifters find the first work set easier after one rep at that weight. Trial evidence for a benefit is thin.
base-term-5x5
Five sets of five (5x5)

A strength routine of five sets of five reps on a few compound lifts, popularised by Bill Starr in a book for football players and revived by later barbell programmes. The label covers several quite different set plans.
base-term-ramp-sets-across
Ramped sets and sets across
Ramped sets rise in weight from set to set, so only the last one or two are hard. Sets across use the same working weight for every set, after separate warm-up sets.
base-5x5-ramp-for-learning
Five rising sets of five suit learning a lift, if someone checks the technique
Each session gives 25 practice reps that end in one challenging set. Without a coach, lifters tend to add weight faster than their form allows.
base-5x5-sets-across
For five sets of five at one weight, use about 75 to 80% of max
A true five-rep max cannot be repeated for five sets. The working weight has to sit below it, and total reps show whether it is right.
base-num-5x5-load
Load that allows five sets of five at one weight
McDonald's working range for 5x5 with the same weight. A single maximal set of five is about 85%.
base-5x5-assessment
What five sets of five does well, and where it falls short
It is a sound way to build base strength and some size. It is not a peaking plan, and it leans on lifts that need coaching.
base-term-20-rep-squat
20-rep squat (breathing squat)
An old rest-pause method: one set of 20 squats with a weight you could normally lift about 10 times, made possible by standing with the bar and taking several deep breaths between reps.
base-20-rep-squat-assessment
The 20-rep squat teaches effort, but its famous weight-gain claims do not hold up
One all-out set shows a lifter how far real limits lie beyond perceived ones. Rapid weight gained on such a plan is not mostly muscle.
base-20-rep-squat-safely
Break in below your 10-rep max and keep a 20-rep squat cycle short
Start 10 to 20% under your best 10-rep weight, add a little each time you make 20, and stop after four to eight weeks.
base-mistake-20-rep-deadlift
Applying the 20-rep grind to deadlifts or good mornings
Technique in these lifts breaks down quickly as reps climb, and the part that fails is the back.
base-term-weider-principles
Weider principles

Names such as the superset, split routine and drop set principles, attached by the publisher Joe Weider to methods lifters already used. They are labels from his magazines, not discoveries; the hypertrophy area covers what the methods do.
The 300, 400, 500 rule is a long-term target for an average-sized man
A strict bench press of 300 lb (136 kg), squat of 400 lb (181 kg) and deadlift of 500 lb (227 kg) is an old estimate of where a drug-free lifter nears his muscular limit.
base-num-mcrobert-ratios
The 300, 400, 500 rule as multiples of body weight
Bench press, squat and deadlift for a man of about 90 kg (200 lb), as McDonald works out McRobert's rule. A coaching target, not a norm.
1.5 / 2 / 2.5 x body weight
base-table-powerlifter-percentiles
Top-tenth relative strength in drug-tested, unequipped powerlifters
90th-percentile lifts for competitors aged 18 to 35, from 809,986 competition entries, beside the McRobert target for an average man.
base-raw-lift-order
In unequipped lifting the deadlift is biggest, then the squat, then the bench press
Norms from over 800,000 drug-tested, unequipped competition entries show that order at the 90th percentile for both sexes.
base-mistake-loose-standards
Comparing your lifts with numbers that carry no conditions
A lift only compares with a standard done the same way: same depth, no bounce or help, same body weight and sex, and no drugs or supportive suits.
base-strength-gain-slows
The stronger you are, the slower strength comes
Across 15 years of competition results, the strongest quarter of men gained strength at about half the daily rate of the least strong quarter.
base-term-process-outcome-goals
Outcome, performance and process goals

An outcome goal is a result against others, such as winning. A performance goal is a standard of your own, such as a 100 kg (220 lb) squat. A process goal is an action you carry out, such as hitting depth on every rep.
base-process-goals-work
Goals about what you do beat goals about what you get
In a meta-analysis of goal setting in sport, process goals improved performance far more than performance or outcome goals.
base-mistake-record-every-session
Judging every session by whether you set a personal best
Records cannot come every time. Treating each ordinary session as a failure builds tension that makes the next one worse.
base-table-control
What a lifter can and cannot control
Lyle McDonald's rule: accept the fixed factors, use them only to shape your approach, and put the effort into the rest.
base-self-coaching-questions
Two questions can stand in for a coach
Ask what you would tell another lifter in your position. And if you are wondering whether to do one more set, take that as a no.
base-mistake-self-coach-adding
Adding sets, sessions and exercises to your own plan as you go
Self-coached lifters rarely fail through laziness. They do too much, too often, and explain to themselves why they are the exception.
base-coach-value
A coach adds technique, restraint and a plan
Supervised lifters gained more strength than unsupervised ones in pooled trials. The benefit is partly being pushed and partly being held back.
base-simple-beats-complex
A simple plan carried out fully beats an elaborate one
Coaches tend to overcomplicate in mid-career and simplify with experience. Evidence agrees that most programme details change little.
base-athlete-look-selection
Sports select body types more than they build them
There is no single athletic physique. Elite athletes look alike within a sport because those with the right build rise to the top.
base-mistake-champion-habit
Picking one habit of champions as the reason for their success
The lifters who got nowhere usually had the same habit. What top performers share is a decade or more of consistent work, plus talent.
base-power-older-adults
Lifting the weight fast adds a little to physical function in older adults
In adults over 60, training with a fast lifting phase improved physical function modestly more than conventional strength training.
base-health-lifting-dose
For general health, two or three short full-body sessions cover the lifting
Guidelines ask for resistance exercise for each major muscle group on two or three days a week. One to three sets of one or two exercises per muscle is enough.
base-health-heavier-sets
Occasional heavier sets and loaded standing lifts are worth including for bone
Bone responds to heavy loading through the skeleton. A health-focused lifter gains from some sets of 5 or 6 without living there.
base-table-health-week
Weekly layouts for all-round fitness
Ways Lyle McDonald arranges lifting and cardio for general fitness, by the days available. All meet the guideline of lifting on two or three days.
base-health-rep-variation
After the first year, vary reps in simple ways
Three easy options: step the reps down over weeks, progress inside one wide rep range, or use two rep ranges in the same week.
tech-bench-general-style
For general training, bench with a part-tucked elbow and pinned shoulder blades
A slight arch, shoulder blades held back and elbows midway between flared and tucked is a sound default for lifters who do not compete.
tech-bench-bar-path
Start and finish each bench rep with the bar stacked over the shoulders
With the arms vertical the skeleton holds the bar. Lower it in a shallow arc to the lower chest and press back along the same arc.
tech-bench-forearms-vertical
Pick a bench grip that puts the forearms vertical at the bottom
Elbows stacked under the bar at the chest send force straight into it. Very wide grips add little load and may add shoulder risk.
tech-num-bench-grip
Bench grip width a review linked to lower shoulder risk
A review found wider grips may raise shoulder injury risk, while narrowing to this width changed the one-rep max by about 5%.
1.5 or less x biacromial width
tech-num-bench-elbow-angle
Upper-arm angle at the bottom of a general-purpose bench press
McDonald's coaching range: arms neither level with the shoulders nor pinned to the ribs. A convention, not a measured optimum.
45-60 degrees from the torso
tech-mistake-bench-flared
Benching to the collarbone with the elbows level with the shoulders
Flaring the elbows fully to isolate the chest puts the shoulder in a position McDonald considers poor value with a heavy bar.
tech-bench-feel-chest
To feel the chest in a press, think of bringing the upper arms together
Focusing on the chest raised chest muscle activity in two lab studies at light and moderate loads, and less reliably at 80% of max.
tech-term-horizontal-adduction
Horizontal adduction
Moving the upper arm across the front of the body toward the midline, as in a dumbbell fly. It is the main action of the chest muscle in every press.
tech-upright-row-height
Stop upright rows when the elbows reach shoulder height
Pulling no higher than shoulder level still works the side of the shoulder and avoids the arm position linked to impingement signs.
tech-num-upright-row-angle
Arm angle above which upright rows were linked to impingement signs
In a case-control study of 77 men, upright rows and lateral raises above this angle were associated with clinical signs of shoulder impingement.
90 degrees
tech-term-impingement
Subacromial impingement
Pinching of tendons and other soft tissue between the top of the upper arm bone and the bony roof of the shoulder as the arm is raised. A clinician makes the diagnosis.
tech-row-finish
Finish every row with the shoulder blades together and the chest up
The mid-back only does its share if the shoulder blades squeeze back as the pull finishes. A one to two second hold keeps that honest.
tech-mistake-row-too-heavy
Rowing so heavy that the chest drops and the body swings back
When the shoulders stay rounded or the torso leans far back, the arms and lower back take over from the mid-back.
tech-table-row-variations
How grip and elbow path change a row
A coaching guide to what each row tends to emphasise. The mid-back works in all of them when the shoulder blades squeeze together.
tech-row-spine-load
Inverted rows load the spine least; bent-over rows work the whole back hardest
In a lab comparison of three rows, the inverted row gave the lowest spine load and the bent-over row the largest back muscle activity.
tech-pulldown-shoulder-blades
In pulldowns and chin-ups, let the shoulders rise, then pull them down
Letting the shoulders lift at the top and drawing them down during the pull turns an arm exercise into a lat exercise.
tech-pulldown-grip-width
Pulldown grip width matters less than gym lore suggests
Lat activity was similar across narrow, medium and wide overhand grips, and the widest grip allowed the least load.
tech-mistake-wide-grip-wide-lats
Using a very wide grip to build wider lats
A grip at twice shoulder width did not raise lat activity over the whole rep and reduced the load lifted.
tech-pulldown-behind-neck
Behind-the-neck pulldowns add nothing for the lats
Lat activity was the same in front, behind-the-neck and V-bar pulldowns, and the study's authors advised against the behind-the-neck version.
tech-term-scapular-retraction
Scapular retraction and depression
Retraction is drawing the shoulder blades back toward the spine. Depression is drawing them down, away from the ears. Rows finish with the first and pulldowns with the second.
tech-checklist-deadlift
Conventional deadlift: set-up and pull
The flat-backed, hip-width deadlift Lyle McDonald teaches general trainees, as coaching checkpoints. No trial compares these cues.
tech-deadlift-bar-height
A deadlift bar loaded with small plates starts too low
The usual start height comes from full-size plates, so lighter lifters need full-diameter light plates or blocks.
tech-mistake-hips-shoot
Hips rising first in a deadlift
If the hips rise before the bar has moved, the legs have straightened without lifting anything and the back must finish the job.
tech-table-deadlift-between-reps
Three ways to string deadlift reps together
How you treat the floor between reps changes what a set trains. The 'suits' column is McDonald's coaching view.
tech-table-deadlift-grips
Deadlift grips compared
Holding strength and trade-offs of the common grips. The ranking is coaching experience; the biceps note comes from an injury video review.
tech-mixed-grip-care
With a mixed grip, keep the underhand elbow straight and swap hands between sets
The mixed grip holds the most weight, and it exposes the biceps tendon of the palm-forward arm.
tech-num-mixed-grip-biceps
Mixed-grip deadlift biceps ruptures that were in the underhand arm
In a review of injury videos, every biceps tendon rupture during a mixed-grip deadlift was in the palm-forward arm. All lifters were men.
24 of 24 ruptures on video
tech-trap-bar
A trap bar deadlift shifts load from the lower back toward the knees
Standing inside a hexagonal bar lowered peak moments at the spine and hip and raised them at the knee in trained lifters.
tech-table-rdl-sldl
Romanian deadlift and stiff-legged deadlift compared
Two lifts that often share a name. Descriptions follow Lyle McDonald's usage; some coaches define the stiff-legged lift with a flat back.
tech-rdl-depth
A Romanian deadlift ends where the hips stop moving
Any depth gained after the hips stop comes from rounding the lower back, which takes the load off the hamstrings.
tech-rdl-programming
Use Romanian deadlifts for moderate reps and build up slowly
Sets of five to eight after the main lift suit most people. Do not test a one-rep max, and expect sore hamstrings at first.
tech-term-rdl
Romanian deadlift (RDL)
A hip hinge started from standing: knees slightly bent, hips pushed back, back flat, bar lowered along the thighs. The name is credited to Romanian weightlifter Nicu Vlad.
tech-term-flexion-relaxation
Flexion-relaxation
The spinal muscles going electrically quiet near a full forward bend, so that ligaments and discs carry more of the load. A review links it to load sharing by passive tissues.
tech-round-back-two-cases
A back that rounds mid-lift is a fault; a set, held upper-back curve is a style
Arguments over round-back deadlifts mix up losing a flat back under load with choosing a fixed upper-back curve before the pull.
tech-lumbar-flexion-evidence
Evidence on lifting with a rounded lower back is mixed and mostly indirect
Tissue studies link repeated loaded bending to disc injury, while a review of people lifting found no clear link between lumbar flexion and back pain.
tech-back-extension-pad
Pad height decides whether a back extension trains the hips or the spinal muscles
With the pad below the hip crease the hips do the moving. With the pelvis pinned on the pad, the spinal muscles must.
tech-mistake-back-extension-overarch
Arching past straight at the top of a back extension
Coming up beyond a straight line adds spine load without adding useful muscle work. Stop when the body is straight.
tech-back-extension-progression
Start back extensions with one easy set and progress in small steps
McDonald starts beginners on a single set of five to eight reps and keeps direct lower-back work well short of failure.
tech-back-endurance
Back muscle endurance was linked to fewer first-time back problems in men
In a Danish population study, men with good isometric back endurance were less likely to report low-back trouble for the first time.
tech-squat-style-choice
Choose a squat style from your goal and your build
A higher bar and upright trunk bias the thighs. A lower bar with more sit-back spreads the work to hips and back and allows more load.
tech-heeled-shoes
A raised heel lets the knees travel forward and the trunk stay more upright
In two lab studies, weightlifting shoes reduced forward lean or increased knee bend compared with ordinary trainers.
tech-squat-build
Some lifters squat upright and some fold forward
Lifters who lean far forward tend to tire in the lower back before the thighs. Ankle mobility is one measured cause; proportions are a likely one.
tech-squat-depth-growth
Full squats grew glutes and inner thighs more than half squats; quadriceps grew the same
Over 10 weeks, deeper squats gave two to three times the glute and adductor growth, with no extra growth at the front of the thigh.
tech-num-squat-depth-glutes
Glute growth from full squats against half squats
MRI change in glute volume in 17 men training twice a week. Quadriceps growth was similar, at 4.9% and 4.6%.
6.7 vs 2.2 % volume in 10 weeks
tech-squat-vs-leg-press
Squats carried over to jumping better than leg presses
Eight weeks of squats raised jump height about 12 percent, against 0.5 to 3.5 percent for the leg press. For thigh size the leg press is a fair substitute.
tech-leg-press-depth
On the leg press, go deep but stop before the pelvis rolls off the pad
Bend the knees to a right angle or more, and treat the point where the lower back starts to round as the bottom.
tech-mistake-everyone-full-squat
Expecting every adult to reach a full-depth barbell squat
Toddlers and people resting in a deep squat are poor guides to what a loaded adult skeleton can do.
tech-split-squat-setup
Set a split squat long enough and wide enough
Both knees should be near a right angle in the low position, with the feet about hip width apart and not on one line.
tech-split-squat-emphasis
Front shin angle steers a split squat toward the thighs or the glutes
Letting the front knee travel forward biases the thigh. A vertical shin with the weight on the heel biases the glutes.
tech-split-squat-vs-squat
Rear-foot-elevated split squats matched back squats over five weeks in young rugby players
Strength, 40 m sprint and agility improved equally whether the players trained only split squats or only back squats.
tech-single-leg-order
In single-leg work, start with the weaker side and rest before switching
Let the weaker leg set the reps for both, and take about a minute between legs so the second one is not short-changed.
tech-calf-pause
Pause at the bottom of calf raises so the muscle does the lifting
The Achilles tendon hands back stored energy when a rep is bounced. A two-second pause in the stretch removes most of that help.
tech-mistake-calf-bounce
Bouncing calf raises through a short range
Fast, springy reps let the Achilles tendon carry part of each lift, so the muscle does less than the load suggests.
tech-calf-standing-vs-seated
Standing calf raises grew the calf far more than seated ones
With the knee straight both calf muscles grew. With the knee bent only the soleus did, and no more than it did standing.
tech-num-calf-standing
Outer calf growth from standing against seated raises
Lateral gastrocnemius growth in 14 untrained adults who trained one leg standing and one seated. Soleus growth was 2.1% and 2.9%.
12.4 vs 1.7 % volume in 12 weeks
tech-term-gastrocnemius-soleus
Gastrocnemius and soleus

The two main calf muscles. The gastrocnemius is the visible one and crosses both knee and ankle. The soleus lies under it and crosses only the ankle, so it does most of the work when the knee is bent.
tech-leg-extension-burn
Why high-rep leg extensions burn so much is not established
McDonald's guess is that the seated, hip-bent position limits blood flow through the thigh for the whole set. Nobody has tested it.
tech-leg-extension-knee-stress
Leg extensions stress the kneecap joint most near straight; squats stress it most deep
A modelling study found opposite patterns: knee extensions loaded the joint behind the kneecap more from 0 to 30 degrees, squats more from 60 to 90.
tech-leg-extension-recline
Leaning back on the leg extension grew the rectus femoris more
With the hips opened to 40 degrees of bend, the thigh muscle that crosses the hip grew more than at 90 degrees. The outer thigh grew the same.
tech-term-patellofemoral
Patellofemoral joint
The joint between the kneecap (patella) and the groove at the end of the thigh bone. How hard it is loaded changes with knee angle and differs between squats and leg extensions.
tech-model-vs-style
Good technique is a shared model with room for personal style
Skilled lifters look broadly alike in a given lift and differ in details that follow from their build.
tech-term-technique-fault
Technique fault
A departure from a lift's general model that build or style does not explain and that limits performance or progress, or raises injury risk. McDonald's working definition; faults come in degrees.
tech-table-fault-sources
Three sources of a technique fault and where to start
A coaching framework drawn from Lyle McDonald's writing on changing technique. A long-standing fault usually involves the third row as well.
tech-external-focus
Cues about the bar or the floor beat cues about body parts for learning a movement
Across dozens of studies, attending to the effect of a movement improved performance and learning more than attending to the limbs.
tech-term-external-focus
External and internal focus

External focus is attention on the effect of a movement, such as the bar's path. Internal focus is attention on body parts, such as squeezing a muscle. Motor-learning research favours external focus for skill.
tech-num-external-focus
Advantage of external over internal focus for retaining a skill
A moderate effect pooled from 40 studies with 1,274 participants. The effect on immediate performance was smaller, 0.26 across 73 studies.
0.58 Hedges' g
tech-old-habit-returns
An old movement habit is overwritten, not erased, and returns under fatigue or pressure
Expect a corrected fault to reappear with heavy loads, late in sets or in competition until the new pattern has been drilled in those conditions.
tech-mistake-load-before-technique
Adding weight before the movement is stable
Reps done wrong still count as practice. The more often a faulty pattern is repeated, the more automatic and the harder to change it becomes.
tech-no-required-exercise
No gym exercise is compulsory unless your sport tests it
Powerlifters, weightlifters and some strongman competitors must squat. For everyone else a lift only has to be safe, load the target and allow progress.
tech-mistake-safe-unsafe-labels
Labelling an exercise simply safe or unsafe
Risk depends on how a lift is done and who is doing it, so weigh the likely benefit against the likely cost for that person.
tech-breathing-basic
New lifters should keep breathing and leave bracing for later
For light, general training, breathe in as you lower and out as you lift. The first job is simply not to hold your breath through a set.
tech-valsalva-brace
A held breath stiffens the trunk for heavy squats and deadlifts
Breathing in and bearing down against a closed throat raises pressure inside the abdomen, which helps keep the spine rigid under heavy loads.
tech-valsalva-blood-pressure
Blood pressure climbs very high in heavy lifts, and higher with a held breath
Direct measurements show pressures above 300/250 mm Hg on maximal leg presses. Exhaling slowly during the lift cut the pressure by over a third.
tech-num-leg-press-bp
Mean peak blood pressure on heavy double-leg presses
Measured inside the artery in five experienced bodybuilders lifting to failure at 80 to 100% of max. One subject exceeded 480/350.
tech-term-valsalva
Valsalva manoeuvre

Trying to breathe out against a closed throat. It raises pressure in the chest and abdomen, which stiffens the trunk and also raises blood pressure. Lifters use a brief, partial version on heavy reps.
tech-term-iap
Intra-abdominal pressure (IAP)
Pressure inside the abdominal cavity. It rises when you hold a breath and tighten the trunk, and a lifting belt raised it further in a deadlift study. It is thought to help support the spine.
tech-table-breathing-patterns
Breathing patterns for a rep, from light to heavy work
Options coaches use, with McDonald's view of where each fits. More held breath means more trunk stiffness and a bigger rise in blood pressure.
tech-brace-each-rep
On heavy sets, breathe and brace again before every rep
Treating a set of five as five singles keeps the brace and the set-up from getting sloppy as the set gets hard.
tech-straps-when
Lift without straps until grip limits you, then strap up
This middle path trains the grip early in the session and stops it from capping the back work that follows.
tech-mistake-grip-limits-back
Letting grip end sets that are meant to train the back
If the hands give out before the back or hamstrings, those muscles finish the set under-trained.
tech-table-grip-aids
Grip aids compared
Common grip aids and where each fits. Closed-loop straps should not be used for cleans, because the bar cannot be released quickly.
tech-rituals-belief
A harmless pre-lift ritual can help, because belief moves performance a little
Placebo effects on sports performance are small to moderate in pooled studies, so a routine you trust is worth keeping if it costs nothing.
tech-jump-hip-extension
A jump is driven by straightening hips, knees and ankles
The hamstrings work at two joints: they bend the knee and they straighten the hip. In jumping, squatting and weightlifting they need to do the second job.
tech-jump-drills
Drills that teach a full, fast hip extension
Rope skipping, kettlebell swings, backward overhead medicine-ball throws and plain vertical jumps all rehearse extending completely.
tech-plyometrics-jump-height
Jump training raises jump height by about 5 to 9 percent
A meta-analysis of 26 studies found plyometric training improved every type of vertical jump tested. Using the arms adds height too.
tech-term-triple-extension
Triple extension
Straightening the hips, knees and ankles together, as at take-off in a jump or at the top of a weightlifting pull.
tech-table-change-worth-it
When a technique fault is worth fixing
McDonald's view by situation. The longer a pattern has been trained and the better it is working, the higher the bar for changing it.
tech-change-costs
Changing a practised technique loads new tissue and can lower performance at first
In running studies, a taught technique cut work at the knee, raised it at the ankle and worsened economy after 12 weeks.
tech-checklist-change-technique
Changing an ingrained technique: a working plan
Coaching steps from Lyle McDonald's two-part guide. They have not been tested as a package; treat them as a sensible order of work.
tech-practice-spacing
Short, frequent practice beats one long session for learning a skill
Spaced practice outperformed massed practice across 63 studies. Mixing drills helps retention in the lab and little in applied settings.
tech-num-reps-correct
Share of reps done correctly before adding load
A rule of thumb McDonald credits to Mel Siff: once about four reps in five are right, raise the load a little. Not a research figure.
80 % of reps
tech-mistake-empty-bar
Stripping back to an empty bar to fix every fault
Too little load can make a lift harder to feel. Go light enough to do it right, not as light as possible.
tech-term-training-age
Training age
How many years a person has been training, as distinct from how old they are. A long training age means a more automatic pattern and tissues adapted to it.
tech-emg-not-growth
Higher muscle activity on EMG does not mean more muscle growth
The hip thrust showed about twice the glute EMG of the squat in one session, yet nine weeks of either grew the glutes the same.
tech-hip-thrust-vs-squat
Hip thrusts and squats grew the glutes equally; squats also grew the thighs
In untrained adults over nine weeks, glute growth was similar with either lift, while quadriceps and adductors grew more with squats.
tech-term-emg
Surface EMG (electromyography)

A recording of a muscle's electrical activity through electrodes on the skin. It shows that a muscle is active during a lift; the size of the signal does not reliably predict strength gains or growth.
tech-checklist-exercise-study
Questions to ask of a study that compares two exercises
Checks drawn from Lyle McDonald's critique of a small hip thrust study. Weak answers to several of them mean the result is a hint at most.
tech-novice-strength-tests
In beginners, strength tests improve with practice and growth shows first in simple lifts
Untrained people who only practised a one-rep max gained as much max strength as people who trained with high volume.
hyp-volume-dose-response
More weekly sets build more muscle, with diminishing returns
Muscle growth rises with weekly hard sets per muscle, but each added set gives less than the one before it.
hyp-volume-range-12-20
12 to 20 weekly sets per muscle is a reasonable range for trained lifters
A review of trained young men found 12-20 sets per muscle per week a sensible target. Treat it as a guide, not a cap.
hyp-volume-any-programme
Almost any structured programme beats no training, and multiple sets rank highest for size
In a network meta-analysis, every prescription beat no exercise, and multi-set programmes ranked highest for hypertrophy.
hyp-effort-closer-to-failure
Sets ended closer to failure tended to build more muscle
In a meta-regression, hypertrophy improved as sets ended nearer to failure, while strength gains were similar across a wide range.
hyp-effort-failure-optional
Going to absolute failure has not shown a clear edge over stopping just short
Training to momentary failure was not clearly better for muscle than stopping close to it.
hyp-effort-rir-accuracy
Reps in reserve is a useful guide, but most lifters misjudge it
RIR tracks how hard a set was, but people tend to underpredict how many reps they have left, by about one rep on average.
hyp-effort-effective-reps-idea
The effective-reps idea is a useful rule of thumb, not a measured law
The idea that only the last few reps near failure drive growth fits the direction of the data. No fixed cut-off has been shown.
hyp-effort-effective-reps-limits
Where the effective-reps model stops working
The model assumes a rep near failure is worth the same at any load and that you can tell which reps those are. Both are shaky.
hyp-load-light-heavy-similar
Light and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are hard
Muscle growth was similar with light and heavy loads when sets were taken close to failure.
hyp-load-strength-heavier
Heavier loads give better strength gains
If one-rep-max strength matters to you, train with heavier loads at least part of the time.
hyp-load-progression-methods
Adding reps and adding weight both work as progression
In new lifters, progressing by reps or by load gave the same strength and muscle gains over 10 weeks.
hyp-freq-volume-matched
With weekly sets matched, training a muscle more often adds little growth
Once total weekly sets are equal, how often you train a muscle makes little difference to size.
hyp-freq-split-vs-full-body
Full-body and split routines give similar results
A meta-analysis found no meaningful difference in strength or muscle size between split and full-body routines.
hyp-rom-full-default
Use a full range of motion by default; lengthened partials also work
Full range of motion is the safe default. Partial reps done in the stretched half held up well in newer trials.
hyp-length-stretched-position
Loading a muscle in its stretched position grew more in several trials
Exercises that load a muscle when it is long gave bigger gains than versions that load it short, in trials that compared them.
hyp-rest-between-sets
Rest long enough to repeat your reps; 2 to 5 minutes gave similar growth in trained men
Longer rest keeps reps up across sets. In trained men, resting 2 or 5 minutes gave similar muscle gains.
hyp-tempo-controlled
Lift under control; very slow reps are not needed
Controlled reps work. Reps of 10 seconds or more are best avoided, and slowing the lowering phase had no clear extra effect on size.
hyp-tech-drop-sets
Drop sets match straight sets for growth and can save time
Drop sets built about the same muscle as normal sets in a pooled analysis, so the case for them is time and variety.
hyp-tech-supersets
Supersets let you do the same work in less time
Supersets gave similar volume and similar strength and size results in shorter sessions.
hyp-tech-rest-pause-cluster
Rest-pause and cluster sets are fatigue and time tools, not growth boosters
Pooled reviews found cluster sets and similar set structures give about the same size and strength as straight sets.
hyp-tech-blood-flow-restriction
Blood-flow restriction can build size with light loads, but needs care
Light loads with a cuff that restricts blood flow built muscle similarly to heavy training, but built less strength.
hyp-prog-exercise-order
Put the exercises that matter most first
Reps and volume are higher for an exercise placed early in a session, and pre-exhaustion gave no extra benefit.
hyp-prog-warm-up
Warm up with lighter sets of the first lift; save long stretches for later
Warming up helps performance. Long static stretches right before lifting can reduce it slightly.
hyp-prog-deload-evidence
Deloads are common practice, but trials do not yet show they are needed
Coaches use deloads regularly. The one small trial in beginners found cutting volume in weeks 4 and 8 neither helped nor hurt.
hyp-prog-periodisation
Periodising your training helps strength more than muscle size
When volume was equal, planned changes in volume and load helped strength but not muscle size.
hyp-prog-early-gains-swelling
Muscle size gains in the first weeks partly reflect swelling
Measured size rises in the first weeks, but some of that early gain is swelling from training stress, not new muscle tissue.
hyp-prog-read-a-study
How to read a training study before you act on it
Check who was studied, for how long, how muscle was measured and how failure was defined before copying a result.
hyp-rec-sleep
Short sleep lowers lifting performance
Sleep loss lowered exercise performance in a large meta-analysis, and one small study found lower muscle protein synthesis after a sleepless night.
hyp-mistake-chasing-soreness
Judging a session by how sore you are
Soreness does not show that a session worked, and its absence does not show that it failed.
hyp-mistake-no-progression
Repeating the same weights and reps with no log
Without a record, you cannot tell whether you are adding reps or load, which is what progression means.
hyp-mistake-cutting-range
Cutting the range of motion to lift heavier
Shortening the rep to add weight tended to give up size in the lower body. Partials in the stretched half are different.
hyp-mistake-stopping-far-from-failure
Ending every set far from failure
Sets that stop well short of failure leave growth on the table, and self-chosen loads are often light.
hyp-mistake-volume-too-fast
Jumping to very high volume straight away
More sets add less each time, so a big jump from your current volume mostly adds fatigue.
hyp-mistake-rest-too-short
Cutting rest so short that your reps fall
Very short rests lower the reps you can do on later sets, and with it the total work.
hyp-num-weekly-sets
Weekly sets per muscle
A range from a review of trained young men; a newer analysis found no clear ceiling.
12-20 sets per muscle per week
hyp-num-rir-error
Average underprediction of reps to failure
Across 12 studies, lifters guessed they had about one rep fewer in the tank than they did.
0.95 reps, average miss
hyp-num-self-selected-load
Load people choose when left alone
Average self-selected load across exercises in a scoping review; light unless sets end near failure.
53 % of 1RM, average
hyp-num-heavy-threshold
Load that maximised strength gains
Loads above this ranked best for strength in a network meta-analysis. All loads comparably built muscle.
80+ % of 1RM
hyp-num-light-threshold
Upper limit of light-load training in a meta-analysis
Training at or below this load built muscle similarly to heavier loads, but built less strength.
60 or less % of 1RM
hyp-num-rest-minutes
Rest between sets with similar growth in trained men
In 13 strength-trained men, 2 and 5 minute rests gave similar muscle gains over three months.
2-5 minutes between sets
hyp-num-deload-interval
Weeks between deloads reported by athletes
Reported by 246 strength and physique athletes. This is what they do, not what trials show is best.
5.6 weeks, average
hyp-num-deload-length
Typical deload length reported by athletes
Average length of a deload in the same survey of 246 strength and physique athletes.
6.4 days, average
hyp-num-sleep-loss
Average performance change after short sleep
Pooled across 69 publications where sleep was 6 hours or less in 24 hours.
-7.6 % performance change
hyp-num-early-thigh-gain
Thigh muscle area gain in 8 weeks, sedentary men
Includes swelling in the first weeks. Typical for new lifters, not for trained ones.
9.6 % over 8 weeks
hyp-term-volume
Volume
The amount of work. In this page, usually the number of hard sets per muscle per week. Volume load is sets times reps times weight.
hyp-term-hard-set
Hard set
A working set taken close to failure, usually within a few reps. Warm-up sets and easy sets do not count towards weekly volume.
hyp-term-momentary-failure
Momentary muscular failure
The point where you cannot finish another rep despite maximal effort. Volitional failure means you stop by choice.
hyp-term-rir
Repetitions in reserve (RIR)
The number of reps you could still have done when the set ended. 0 RIR means failure. 2 RIR means two more reps were possible.
hyp-term-rpe
Rate of perceived exertion (RPE)
A 1-10 effort scale. On the RIR-based version, RPE 10 means 0 RIR, RPE 9 means 1 RIR, and so on.
hyp-term-1rm
One-rep max (1RM)
The heaviest load you can lift for one full rep. Training loads are often given as a percent of it, such as 70% of 1RM.
hyp-term-progressive-overload
Progressive overload

Gradually asking more of the muscle over time, by adding reps, load or sets, so it keeps having a reason to adapt. Adding reps up to the top of a range and then adding weight is called double progression.
hyp-term-deload
Deload
A period of reduced training stress meant to lower fatigue and prepare you for later training, as defined by a coach consensus.
hyp-term-lengthened
Lengthened-position training
Loading a muscle while it is stretched, as at the bottom of a curl or squat. Several trials found it grew more than loading it short.
hyp-term-effect-size
Effect size and confidence interval
Effect size is how big a difference is, in standard deviations. The interval shows a plausible range. If it spans zero, there is no clear difference.
hyp-term-periodisation
Periodisation
Planned changes in volume, load or exercises over weeks and months, such as linear steps or weekly undulation.
hyp-table-rep-ranges
Rep ranges and what each is good for
Approximate loads for each rep range. Growth was similar across loads in pooled trials, so 8-12 is a handy middle, not a special range. Percentages vary by person and lift.
hyp-table-splits
Training splits compared
Splits differ in how often each muscle is trained and how the week is arranged. With weekly volume equal, growth was similar in pooled trials.
hyp-table-rest-and-sets
Rest between sets and sets per week: a guide
A reading of the research on rest and weekly sets. Treat each line as a starting point, then adjust to how you recover.
hyp-term-mechanotransduction
Mechanotransduction
How a muscle fibre senses physical tension and converts it into chemical signals for growth. A 2011 review puts mTOR signalling at the centre of this response to load.
hyp-term-mtor
mTOR (mTORC1)

A protein kinase complex in muscle cells that helps switch on protein synthesis in response to loading. In a human trial, blocking it with the drug rapamycin stopped the early rise in synthesis after hard contractions.
hyp-term-size-principle
Size principle (orderly recruitment)

Motor units join a contraction in order of size: small, low-force units first, large, high-force units last, as the force needed rises or earlier units tire. So the largest units work mainly under heavy loads or late in hard sets.
hyp-term-rate-coding
Recruitment and rate coding

The two ways a muscle grades its force. Recruitment adds motor units; rate coding fires active ones faster. In one study the biceps kept recruiting to high forces, while a small thumb muscle finished early and relied more on firing rate.
hyp-num-biceps-recruitment
Force up to which the biceps kept adding motor units
Single-unit recordings found new biceps units joining up to this force. In a small thumb muscle, none joined above 50%.
88 % of maximal isometric force
hyp-volume-extreme-fluid
At extreme volumes, part of the lean mass gained was fluid
When trained men ramped up to 32 sets per exercise a week, most of the late lean-mass gain vanished once extra water outside the cells was accounted for.
hyp-mistake-retracted-volume-trials
Citing the retracted Barbalho trials as proof of a volume ceiling
Two trials whose titles claimed an upper threshold or ceiling for training volume have been retracted. They are not evidence either way.
hyp-term-moment-arm
Moment arm and torque

A moment arm is the perpendicular distance from a joint to the line along which a force acts. Torque, the turning effect at the joint, is force times moment arm, so a weight held farther from the joint is harder to move.
hyp-mistake-compare-exercise-loads
Assuming the exercise with more weight on the bar loads the muscle more
McDonald's view: bar weight tracks muscle tension only within one lift for one person. Between exercises, moment arms and shared work change the picture.
hyp-compound-first-to-fail
In a compound lift, the muscle that tires first decides when the set ends
McDonald's view: if a helper muscle gives out first, the muscle you want to grow may end the set well short of a hard effort.
hyp-table-plate-jumps
How big a fixed weight jump is on heavy and light lifts
The same added weight is a small step on a heavy lift and a big one on a light lift. McDonald's fix for isolation lifts, and for women whose loads are lighter, is small plates.
hyp-load-form-holds
Add weight only while form and range hold; drop it when they slip
McDonald's view: a heavier weight raises tension on the target muscle only if the lift still looks the same, and a lighter weight done properly can load it more.
hyp-prog-load-pace-by-level
Past the first years, expect to add load every few weeks, not every week
McDonald's view: beginners can add weight most sessions, largely from learning the lift, while after two or three years a jump every 4 to 6 weeks is realistic.
hyp-rec-row-vs-curl
Curls tired the elbow flexors more, and for longer, than rows
In 16 highly trained men, 8 hard sets of preacher curls cut elbow-flexor strength more and for longer than rows did. That fits giving a row only part credit for the arms.
hyp-num-light-load-tonnage
Tonnage of heavy sets against light sets to failure
On the tonnage McDonald quotes for a trial in 49 trained men, heavy sets (75-90% of 1RM, 8-12 reps) moved this share of what light sets of 20-25 did. Growth was similar.
62 % of light-set tonnage
hyp-volume-sets-as-measure
Counting hard sets is a fair volume measure across about 6 to 20-plus reps
A review of trials in trained adults found that sets taken to or near failure seem an adequate measure of training volume when each set has between about 6 and 20+ reps.
hyp-voluntary-activation
In two small studies, the biceps was driven almost fully and the quadriceps a little less
Twitch tests found near-full activation of the elbow flexors in 11 subjects and 88 to 95% in the quadriceps of 8 men, not the small share of muscle often claimed.
hyp-load-light-sets-discomfort
Half-load sets to failure took three times as long and felt worse in one trial
Back-extension sets at 50% of maximal force took about three times the reps and time of 80% sets and were rated more uncomfortable. A study at 30% found no difference.
hyp-effort-failure-every-session
Failure in every session grew less than percentage training in one small trial
Well-trained men who took each exercise to failure three days a week gained less fibre size than men training by percentages. McDonald describes the sets and days as matched.
hyp-bodybuilder-fibre-force
Bodybuilders' fibres were the largest but made the least force for their size
In single thigh fibres, bodybuilders' were far bigger than power athletes', yet produced less force per unit of area than either power athletes' or control subjects'.
hyp-responders-fibre-size
Trained men with smaller fast-twitch fibres at the start grew more on one plan
In 30 trained college-aged men on six weeks of high-volume training, a higher share of type II fibres and smaller type II fibres at the start went with more growth.
hyp-num-responder-spread
Change in size for the top and bottom responders to one six-week plan
The 10 best and 10 worst of 30 trained young men on identical high-volume training: one group grew clearly, the other lost a little.
+10.7 and -2.1 % change, 4 thigh measures
hyp-term-satellite-cells
Satellite cells

Stem cells that sit against the outside of each muscle fibre. Once activated they can divide and donate nuclei. In 15 young men their count rose 31% over 90 days of heavy training and was still raised 60 days after stopping, but not at 90.
hyp-term-myonuclear-domain
Myonuclear domain

The share of a fibre served by one nucleus. In 15 young men it grew over 90 days of heavy training with no rise in nuclei and returned to baseline after stopping, so moderate growth needed no new nuclei.
hyp-fibre-number-steroid-users
Signs of new muscle fibres were commoner in steroid-using powerlifters than drug-free ones
Trapezius biopsies from high-level powerlifters showed more markers of fibre formation in those who reported years of steroid use than in those who had never used.
hyp-hormones-arm-trials
Two arm trials disagree on whether a hormone-raising leg session adds growth
A hard leg session raised blood hormones around arm training. One trial found no extra arm growth; a smaller one, with legs trained first, found some.
hyp-num-testosterone-window
How long testosterone stayed raised after exercise
Across 48 studies in men, testosterone rose after moderate or hard exercise when measured within 30 minutes, not later. Light activity did not raise it.
30 minutes or less
hyp-mistake-squats-for-upper-body
Squatting to make your upper body grow through a hormone boost
The testosterone rise after hard exercise is brief. McDonald's view is that chest and arms grow from the work they do themselves; the trials are mixed.
hyp-growth-hormone-strength
Growth hormone raised lean mass but not strength in fit young people
In a systematic review of controlled trials, healthy young people given growth hormone gained lean mass, but strength and exercise capacity did not seem to improve.
hyp-heavy-low-volume-proteins
Heavy low-volume training did not raise muscle energy proteins in one small trial
Ten weeks of heavy, low-volume lifting grew type II fibres in 15 trained men without the rise in energy-system proteins this lab saw after very high volume.
hyp-prog-heavy-then-light
McDonald pairs heavier sets with lighter, short-rest sets for the same muscle
His hypertrophy plans open each muscle with a few heavier sets, then add higher-rep sets on short rests. It is his practice, not a tested rule.
hyp-term-concurrent-periodisation
Concurrent periodisation

Training several qualities, such as speed, maximal strength and size, every week, shifting which one leads. Often called conjugate periodisation, which McDonald says is not what that term first meant.
hyp-prog-strength-block
A spell of low-rep strength work may raise the loads you later use for size
McDonald's view is that a phase of heavy sets of five or fewer builds strength that lets you use more weight in later higher-rep work.
hyp-split-legs-before-pull
McDonald keeps hard back work off the day before squats or deadlifts
His view is that a tired upper back limits squats, deadlifts and Romanian deadlifts, so he orders a split to keep heavy pulling off the day before them.
hyp-split-triceps-long-head
The long head of the triceps also works on pulling days
It crosses the shoulder and helps draw the arm down and back. McDonald's view is that rows and pulldowns therefore work it too, though less directly than presses.
hyp-split-rotating-calendar
Starting a rotating split without checking how sessions fall over two weeks
Three workouts rotated over four training days land on different weekdays each week, so a poor pairing may only show up every other week.
hyp-prog-three-dials
McDonald: a plan that raises volume, effort or frequency must give ground on another
McDonald's view is that well-known hypertrophy plans differ mainly in which of the three they push, and end up in a similar place over a couple of years.
hyp-term-strategic-deconditioning
Strategic deconditioning

A planned week or so off, used in one popular plan to undo the repeated bout effect so muscle responds afresh. McDonald's view is that it fails. In an indirect test, 14 young men taking three-week breaks grew as much as continuous trainers.
hyp-effort-bar-speed-slows
Rep speed drops well before the end of a bench or squat set taken to failure
In bench and squat sets to failure, bar speed fell well before the last rep. McDonald's view is that when every rep moved at the same speed, the set most likely ended short of failure.
hyp-term-muscular-exhaustion
Muscular exhaustion

The state in which a muscle can produce no useful force at all. Failure on a set is narrower: the muscle can no longer meet that load but could still move a lighter one. Lifting sets almost never reach exhaustion.
hyp-term-failure-types
Concentric, isometric and eccentric failure

Being unable to lift the weight, to hold it still, or to lower it under control. A muscle can lower more than it holds and hold more than it lifts, so they come in that order. Nearly all sets stop at concentric failure.
pl-heavy-loads-for-strength
Heavy loads build strength better than light loads
For strength, heavy and moderate loads beat light loads, so most working sets should sit in the heavy to moderate range.
pl-specificity-technique
Practise the lifts in competition style and hold four principles
Strength in the squat, bench press and deadlift is partly skill, so the lifts themselves, done to competition standard, make up most of the training.
pl-rpe-scale
RPE with reps in reserve lets you pick the load by feel
A set rated RPE 9 left one repetition in reserve and RPE 10 left none; the scale worked on all three lifts in powerlifters.
pl-autoregulation
Loading by RPE or bar speed works about as well as percentages
Trials and a meta-analysis found no clear strength difference between autoregulated loading and fixed-percentage loading.
pl-velocity-loss
Velocity loss limits did not change strength gains in a large review
Ending a set when bar speed has dropped by a set percentage is a valid way to cap fatigue; the threshold changed strength little.
pl-not-to-failure
Strength does not need sets taken to failure
Stopping sets short of failure gave similar strength gains to failure training, so heavy work can end with repetitions in reserve.
pl-volume-dose
More weekly sets build more strength, with sharply diminishing returns
Strength rises with weekly sets and with training frequency, but the gains flatten faster than muscle growth does.
pl-minimum-dose
A small dose of heavy work can still raise a powerlifter's 1RM
About 3 to 6 heavy working sets per lift each week was enough to expect strength gains in powerlifters over 6 to 12 weeks.
pl-frequency-by-level
Training days per week usually rise with level
Beginners do well on 2 to 3 sessions a week; advanced lifters often spread the lifts across 4 to 6.
pl-periodised-beats-not
Planned variation beats a fixed routine for 1RM strength
Periodised programs raised 1RM more than non-periodised ones, including when total volume was matched.
pl-linear-block-undulating
Linear, block and undulating plans differ little in trials
No clear winner between linear and undulating models; too few trials exist to compare block models.
pl-taper
Lifters taper for 5 to 10 days by cutting volume and keeping heavy singles
Surveys report a short step taper: volume down about 40-50%, intensity kept high, last heavy squat and deadlift 7-10 days out.
pl-deload
Most strength athletes deload for about a week every 5 to 6 weeks
Deloading is common but little tested: athletes cut sets and load, keep frequency and exercises, and add reps in reserve.
pl-squat-technique
Low-bar squats lean forward and load the hips; high-bar squats stay upright
Bar position changes the squat: low-bar uses more hip and back, high-bar more knee and quadriceps.
pl-bench-technique
Build the bench from the setup: tight back, planted feet, paused bar
A stable arch and tight upper back shorten the bar path and make the pause on the chest repeatable.
pl-deadlift-technique
Sumo and conventional deadlifts load the joints differently
Sumo uses a wide stance and a more upright trunk; conventional moves the bar farther and does more mechanical work.
pl-leverages
Limb and torso lengths change which set-up suits you
Proportions shift the best stance, depth and grip, so copy principles from top lifters and not their exact positions.
pl-accessory-selection
Choose accessories for the point where the lift slows or fails
Find where the bar slows, then train the muscles and positions that fail there with 1 to 3 exercises.
pl-bands-chains
Bands and chains help trained lifters when loads are 80% of 1RM or more
In a meta-analysis, variable resistance beat constant resistance for trained lifters at 80% of 1RM and above.
pl-weight-class-choice
Pick the class you can hold in training; move up when cutting costs lifts
A lifter whose normal weight sits at a class limit can compete there with little cutting; large cuts are a reason to move up.
pl-cut-risks
Rapid weight cuts are common in powerlifting, and fluid loss costs strength
Many lifters cut weight, mostly by fluid methods; fluid loss lowers strength and can harm health.
pl-sleep
Short sleep lowers performance, with evening sessions hit harder
A meta-analysis found sleep loss cut exercise performance by about 7.6% on average.
pl-injury-picture
Injury rates look low, but most lifters report pain in the back, shoulder or hip
Counted as time lost, injuries are infrequent; counted as pain that affects training, most lifters have one.
pl-mistake-max-often
Testing a true max every few weeks
Frequent max attempts add fatigue and risk without adding much information.
pl-mistake-stale-percentages
Running percentages off an old or lucky max
A percentage is only as good as the max behind it, so reset the number when strength changes.
pl-mistake-rpe-guess
Treating RPE as exact when most lifters misjudge reps in reserve
People tend to underpredict reps left in the tank, so RPE is a rough guide that improves with practice.
pl-mistake-cut-fluids
Cutting weight with fluid restriction in the last days
Fluid restriction is a common but risky way to make weight, and it lowers strength and endurance.
pl-mistake-late-changes
Changing technique, equipment or exercises in the final weeks
Late novelty brings soreness and risk with no time to adapt; keep the final weeks specific and familiar.
pl-num-reps-90
Repetitions possible at 90% of 1RM
Typical maximum reps at 90% 1RM across exercises; the bench press averaged about 4.
~5 reps (most lifts)
pl-num-reps-70-bench
Repetitions possible at 70% of 1RM on the bench
Typical maximum reps for the bench press at 70% 1RM; about 9 at 80% and about 4 at 90%.
~14 reps (bench press)
pl-num-rep-spread
Spread in reps between lifters at 80% of 1RM
The between-lifter standard deviation at 80% 1RM is 2.51 reps, so the same percentage gives different rep counts.
2.5 reps (SD)
pl-num-taper-volume
Volume cut during a taper
Surveyed North American powerlifters cut volume by 41-50%; a review of self-reported tapers gave about 40-45%.
40-50 % less volume
pl-num-last-heavy
Last heavy squat and deadlift before a meet
Most surveyed North American raw lifters did their final heavy squat and deadlift 7 to 10 days out; bench came later.
7-10 days before the meet
pl-num-min-dose
Weekly working sets for a minimum effective dose
A floor proposed for powerlifters: 3 to 6 sets of 1 to 5 reps per lift, at loads above 80% 1RM, for 6 to 12 weeks.
3-6 sets per lift per week
pl-num-deload-length
Typical deload length
Average deload length reported by 246 competitive strength and physique athletes, taken about every 5.6 weeks.
6.4 days (every 5.6 weeks)
pl-num-cut-prevalence
Lifters who cut weight at the 2018 IPF classic worlds
Cutters lost an average of 2.9% of body mass; most reported negative mood effects.
83 % of 64 lifters
pl-num-hypohydration
Strength lost with hypohydration
Average fall in muscle strength with hypohydration in a meta-analysis of 28 manuscripts; endurance fell 8.3%.
5.5 % lower muscle strength
pl-num-peak-age
