Mean age of peak performance in world-class powerlifters
From world championship results 2003-2017; powerlifters peaked about 9 years later than weightlifters.
35 years (SD 7)
pl-term-1rm
One-repetition maximum (1RM)
The heaviest weight you can lift once with legal technique; the base for percentage programming.
pl-term-training-max
Working max (training max)
A weight you can repeat on a normal day, often set below a true max, and used as the base for training percentages.
pl-term-rpe
Rating of perceived exertion (RPE)
A 1 to 10 rating of how hard a set was; in strength training it is tied to how many repetitions were left.
pl-term-rir
Repetitions in reserve (RIR)
How many more clean repetitions you could have done when the set ended; 2 RIR means two more were possible.
pl-term-vbt
Velocity-based training (VBT)
Setting load or stopping sets from measured bar speed, using a device that reports mean concentric velocity in metres per second.
pl-term-dup
Daily undulating periodisation (DUP)
A plan that varies rep ranges and loads between sessions within the week, such as heavy, medium and light days.
pl-term-accessory
Accessory exercise
An exercise outside the three competition lifts, chosen to build a muscle or fix a weak point.
pl-term-taper
Taper (peaking)
A planned drop in training stress, mostly volume, in the last days or weeks before a meet so fatigue clears and strength shows.
pl-term-deload
Deload
A planned lighter week or block, with less volume or load, to clear fatigue between harder blocks.
pl-term-sticking-point
Sticking point
The position in a lift where the bar slows most or where failures happen.
pl-table-intensity-zones
Intensity zones as a percent of 1RM
Common coaching zones with typical reps per set and their purpose; reps at a given percentage vary by lifter.
pl-table-rpe-rir
RPE to reps in reserve chart
RPE 5 to 10 matched to repetitions in reserve (RIR); 9.5 is a half step many lifters add.
pl-table-12-week
A 12-week cycle outline
A common layout from base volume to meet week; adjust loads by RPE and your own recovery.
pl-pause-costs-rebound
A pause on the chest takes away the rebound that helps a touch-and-go bench
Pressing straight out of the lowering adds force from the stretch. When the bar sits still, that help fades within a second or two, so a paused bench moves less weight.
pl-term-ssc
Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)

A muscle stretched under load and then shortened at once makes more force than one starting from still. Elastic recoil of tendons and extra time to build force are the usual explanations, and a pause lets the effect fade.
pl-deadlift-dead-start
The first deadlift rep starts cold, so reset reps match the meet
A pull from the floor has no lowering before it. Later reps in a set borrow a stretch from the controlled descent, which the single you pull at a meet never gets.
pl-eight-sets-trained-men
In trained men, eight sets of squats beat one set within three weeks
Squat 1RM rose on one, four or eight sets at 80% to failure, but the eight-set group was ahead of the one-set group by week 3 and stayed ahead.
pl-term-daily-max
Daily max

The heaviest single a lifter can make on that particular day, which may sit above or below their best ever. Working up to it is the core of the Bulgarian weightlifting method, which McDonald says broke most lifters who tried it.
pl-term-bulgarian
Bulgarian method

A weightlifting system associated with coach Ivan Abadjaev: about six exercises, mostly singles to a daily max, over several short sessions a day. McDonald says it suited only full-time, drug-assisted elite lifters and broke most of them.
pl-bulgarian-mcdonald-view
McDonald argues daily maxing does not carry over from weightlifting to powerlifting
His view: a weightlifting max is a split-second explosive effort well short of maximal force, while a squat, bench or deadlift max grinds for seconds and costs far more.
pl-mistake-daily-max
Copying weightlifters' daily maxes into the squat, bench and deadlift
McDonald's view is that near-max singles in the powerlifts every day break most lifters who try them without years of build-up, and that connective tissue is usually what gives out.
pl-imagery
Mental rehearsal raised strength in healthy adults, but less than real training
Across 13 studies, rehearsing a movement in the mind raised maximal strength more than doing nothing, and physical training raised it more than imagery.
pl-term-coactivation
Antagonist coactivation

Firing of the muscle that opposes a movement, such as the hamstrings in knee extension. It steadies the joint but costs net force. In one small study of sedentary men training knee extension isometrically, it fell by a fifth in a week.
pl-heavy-work-in-volume-block
In a high-volume block, keep a little heavy work so top-end strength holds
McDonald's practice is to open sessions in a muscle-building block with a heavy single or triple at about 80 to 90% of max, then do the volume work.
pl-daily-max-evidence
Two small studies of daily maxing point in opposite directions
Three lifters who maxed the squat daily for five weeks gained 2 to 11%. Eleven trained men lifting 100% of 1RM daily on a squat machine lost about 12 kg (27 lb) in two weeks.
pl-strength-heritability
Genes and environment count about equally in strength differences between untrained people
Heritability estimates for strength average about 0.5. That describes differences within a group, not a fixed ceiling for any one lifter.
pl-response-spread
On the same 12-week plan, arm strength gains ranged from none to more than double
In 585 men and women who trained one arm on the same 12-week programme, 1RM gains ran from 0 to 250%, and some barely changed muscle size.
pl-term-deliberate-practice
Deliberate practice

Effortful practice aimed at a specific weakness, often set by a coach, as opposed to repetition on autopilot. A 2016 meta-analysis found it accounted for 18% of the variance in sports performance, and 1% among elite athletes.
pl-warm-ups-as-practice
Treat warm-up sets as focused technique practice, not filler
McDonald's view is that warm-up reps done with full attention to position and bar path add up to a large amount of practice over a year.
pl-num-pause-half-life
Half-life of the rebound effect while the bar is paused
In 12 experienced male lifters benching 95% of max, the extra force from the lowering phase halved for about every 0.85 s the bar was held still.
0.85 seconds
meet-step-choose-federation
Choose a federation: tested or untested sets who you lift against
Tested federations drug test lifters; untested ones do not. The federation also sets your rules, classes and gear list.
meet-step-register-class
Register, then pick a class you can reach by normal eating
Join the federation, enter the meet by its deadline and choose a class near your normal weight.
meet-step-gear
Buy legal gear early and train in it
In IPF rules you need a singlet, a T-shirt under it, shoes and shin-length socks for the deadlift; belt, sleeves and wraps are optional.
meet-step-plan-attempts
Plan nine attempts with your coach or a trusted friend
Plan an opener you could lift easily on any day, a realistic second, and a hard but makeable third.
meet-step-taper
Taper over the last week or two: less volume, a few heavy singles
Survey data show a step taper with 41-50% less volume, the last heavy squat and deadlift 7-10 days out, and rest in the last days.
meet-step-week-logistics
Confirm the schedule, travel and food for the meet
Know your session, weigh-in time and flight, and have travel and meals sorted before the last days.
meet-step-day-before
Lay out gear, eat familiar food and sleep as normally as you can
Eat meals that you know sit well, drink fluids steadily and avoid new foods or heavy training.
meet-step-weigh-in
Weigh in about two hours before lifting, with ID and your opening attempts
IPF and USA Powerlifting weigh-ins run for 90 minutes and start two hours before lifting; the USPA can offer one up to 24 hours before.
meet-step-equipment-check
Pass the equipment check and sign the rack height sheet
Referees inspect and approve each item you plan to wear; an illegal item found later can disqualify you.
meet-step-eat-after
Eat and drink steadily after weigh-in, using food you know
After weigh-in, eat a familiar meal and sip fluids, then keep snacks nearby for the rest of the day.
meet-step-warm-up-room
Time your warm-up from the flight order, not the clock
Work backwards from your opener: count the lifters ahead of you and finish your last warm-up a few lifters before your call.
meet-step-squat
Squat: wait for the command, reach depth, wait for 'rack'
After unracking, stand still with knees locked and wait for 'Squat'; squat below parallel, stand up, then wait for 'Rack'.
meet-step-bench
Bench: wait for 'start', pause on the chest, wait for 'press'
Lock the elbows and wait for 'Start'; lower the bar to your chest, hold still, wait for 'Press', then press and wait for 'Rack'.
meet-step-deadlift
Deadlift: pull to a full lockout and wait for 'down'
Stand erect with knees locked and shoulders back and wait for 'Down'; then lower the bar with control.
meet-step-between-lifts
Between flights: small snacks, fluids, and caffeine only if tried
Eat and drink in small amounts between lifts and try any caffeine in training first.
meet-step-after
After the meet: results, food, rest and a review
Collect your results, eat and rest, and review what the attempts taught you before you plan the next cycle.
meet-federations-differ
Classes, gear lists and drug testing differ between federations
IPF has 8 classes per sex; USA Powerlifting and the USPA list 12 each; check the one you will enter.
meet-lights-and-cards
Three referees show white or red lights, then cards give the reason
White means good lift and red means no lift; after the lights come up, cards show why a lift was turned down.
meet-changing-attempts
You can change an opener once; second attempts and bench or squat thirds are locked
You submit each next weight within one minute of the lights; after that, changes are tightly limited.
meet-caffeine
Caffeine gave a small strength gain in upper-body lifts
A meta-analysis of 10 strength studies found a small gain overall, clearer for upper-body strength.
meet-first-meet-goals
Aim for nine good lifts and a smooth day, not a personal record
A first meet is practice for the whole day: weigh-in, warm-ups, commands and timing.
meet-tested-vs-untested
Tested meets use drug testing; untested meets may not
A federation or meet name tells you which one it is; tested and untested results are kept separate.
meet-mistake-greedy-opener
Opening with a weight that is nearly a max
An opener that is hard to lift risks all three attempts and the total. At a first meet, open lighter, at about 85% of your best single or a little less.
meet-mistake-unchecked-gear
Arriving with gear you never checked against the rulebook
Gear that is not on the list, is too long or too thick, or is torn gets rejected at the equipment check.
meet-mistake-warm-up-timing
Missing your call because the warm-up ran long
You have one minute to start your attempt after the bar is called ready; a late start forfeits it.
meet-mistake-new-food
Trying new food or a big meal after weigh-in
A large or unfamiliar meal after weigh-in can leave you full or ill when the first squat comes.
meet-num-opener
Opener as a share of your current best single
First meet: about 80-85% on squat, 80-82.5% on bench. Squat openers averaged 92% of the day's best in Australian raw meets; elite lifters, 91% of their planned third.
80-85 % of best single
meet-num-second
Second attempt as a share of your current best single
First meet: about 87-92% or a best triple on squat, 85-90% on bench. Elite classic lifters went up about 5% from opener to second.
85-92 % of best single
meet-num-third
Third attempt as a share of your current best single
First meet: about 95% (a best double) on squat, 92-95% on bench, not a max attempt. Elite classic lifters added about 3% from second to third.
92-95 % of best single
meet-num-weigh-in-window
Weigh-in start before lifting
IPF: no earlier than two hours before the category starts. USA Powerlifting: weigh-in starts two hours before lifting.
2 hours before lifting
meet-num-weigh-in-length
Length of the weigh-in period
IPF: one and a half hours. USA Powerlifting: 90 minutes, ending 30 minutes before lifting. USPA: at least 90 minutes.
90 minutes
meet-num-time-to-start
Time to start an attempt after being called
IPF: one minute from the speaker's call to the start of the attempt; USPA also gives one minute.
1 minute
meet-num-increment
Minimum step between attempts
IPF weights are multiples of 2.5 kg, rising at least 2.5 kg between attempts; a missed weight can be repeated. USA Powerlifting uses 2.5 kg increments.
meet-num-leave-platform
Time to leave the platform after an attempt
IPF and USA Powerlifting: leave the platform within 30 seconds of the end of an attempt.
30 seconds
meet-term-opener
Opener (first attempt)
The first of your three attempts on a lift; chosen to be easy enough that you lift it with room to spare.
meet-term-flight
Flight (group)
A group of lifters who take their attempts together; larger sessions split into flights, with lower previous totals lifting first in IPF rules.
meet-term-lot-number
Lot number
A number drawn at weigh-in; if two lifters choose the same weight, the lower lot number lifts first.
meet-term-classic
Classic (raw)
A division with a non-supportive singlet and no supportive suits, shirts or knee wraps; belt, knee sleeves and wrist wraps are allowed within limits.
meet-term-chief-referee
Chief referee
The referee who gives the commands on the platform; two side referees also judge each lift.
meet-term-loaders
Spotter/loaders
Helpers who load the bar and spot squat and bench; two to five are on the platform at a time in IPF rules.
meet-term-rack-height
Rack height sheet
The form where you record squat and bench rack and foot-block settings at weigh-in, so loaders set them before your attempt.
meet-term-bomb-out
Bomb out
To miss all three attempts on a lift; in a full-power meet that usually means no total.
meet-table-ipf-classes
IPF weight classes for men and women, in kg and lb
IPF classes from the 2026 Technical Rules Book; pounds are converted from the kilogram limits.
meet-table-commands
Platform commands for each lift
Commands as given by the chief referee in IPF, USA Powerlifting and USPA rules; wait for each one.
meet-table-attempts
Attempt selection ranges, first meet and experienced
Ranges as a share of a current best single, with a 200 kg (441 lb) example. Experienced rows follow meet data; first-meet rows follow McDonald, as no study covers first meets.
meet-checklist-bag
Meet bag checklist
Pack in the days before the meet, and check the rules of your federation for each item.
meet-mistake-early-commands
Moving before the chief referee's command
Under IPF and USPA rules, lowering the bench before 'Start', pressing before 'Press' or racking before 'Rack' fails the lift, however easily the weight went up.
meet-rehearse-platform
Rehearse the platform in training: commands, no mirror, a referee in front
A meet takes away the rack, the mirror and your usual gym. McDonald has lifters practise the commands for weeks and train some sets with those cues removed.
meet-bench-liftoff
Plan your bench lift-off: who may hand you the bar depends on the federation
Under IPF rules the platform spotter/loaders may unrack the bar for you, and must bring it to arm's length. The USPA also allows your own lift-off person, who must then leave the platform.
meet-final-run-through
A light run-through of the three lifts a day or two out, not a full week off
McDonald's practice is a short session one or two days before the meet: squat, bench and deadlift in order, up to the last warm-up, under full commands.
cond-three-determinants
Endurance performance rests on VO2 max, threshold and efficiency
Three things set endurance performance: peak oxygen uptake, the share of it you can sustain, and how much speed each unit of oxygen buys.
cond-term-functional-threshold
Functional threshold

The hardest pace or power you can hold steadily for about an hour. Lab names for nearby points include maximal lactate steady state and the second lactate threshold. Above it, fatigue builds within minutes.
cond-num-ftp-from-20-minutes
Threshold power estimated from a 20-minute effort
Cycling convention as McDonald describes it. A scoping review found the 20-minute test reliable but not interchangeable with lab markers.
95 % of best 20-min power
cond-table-aerobic-share-track
Aerobic share of energy in track races from 200 m to 1500 m
Measured in 20 highly trained runners on a treadmill. Even a 400 m race drew more than 40% of its energy from aerobic metabolism.
cond-aerobic-base-repeated-efforts
Aerobic fitness supports repeated hard efforts in stop-and-go sports
Recovery between sprints leans on the aerobic system, so basic aerobic work earns a place in team and combat sports.
cond-mistake-lactic-acid
Blaming lactic acid for the burn and for fatigue
Lactate marks hard effort. A biochemistry review argues that producing it slows acid build-up instead of causing it.
cond-no-single-best-intensity
No single intensity trains every part of endurance
Easy volume, threshold work and intervals stress different parts of the system, so McDonald argues none can be the one best intensity.
cond-easy-volume-needs-hours
Easy aerobic training pays off through volume
Elite endurance athletes do about 80% of sessions easy, but they train 10 or more times a week. A few easy hours do far less.
cond-num-elite-low-intensity-share
Share of elite endurance sessions done at low intensity
Typical in studies of athletes training 10 to 13 times a week. The other 20% is dominated by hard work such as intervals.
80 % of sessions
cond-term-polarized
Polarized and pyramidal training

Polarized training puts most sessions at easy effort and a small share at hard interval effort, with little in between. Pyramidal training also starts from a large easy base but keeps more work in the middle zone than at the top.
cond-polarized-not-clearly-better
Polarized training has not clearly beaten other intensity splits
Pooled trials show similar time-trial results for polarized and other splits. Recreational athletes may do as well or better on pyramidal.
cond-volume-intensity-trade
The more often you train, the easier most sessions must be
McDonald's rule: plenty of training time means mostly easy work, and little time means harder steady work. High volume and high intensity do not mix.
cond-mistake-every-session-medium-hard
Doing every session at the same moderately hard effort
Easy days drift too fast and hard days fall short, so everything lands near threshold effort.
cond-term-tempo
Tempo (intensive endurance)

Steady work in the upper aerobic range: clearly harder than easy pace, yet still a steady state that you could hold for an hour or two. Cyclists call it tempo. Sprint coaches use the same word for sub-maximal repeat runs.
cond-term-sweet-spot
Sweet spot training

Andrew Coggan's name for steady work between tempo and threshold effort, usually done in blocks of 10 to 20 minutes with rests half as long. It gives a large aerobic stimulus for the time and is too demanding for beginners.
cond-threshold-small-dose
Threshold sessions work in small doses
Classic threshold work is 20 to 40 minutes at your one-hour pace, once a week. McDonald keeps it to about a tenth of training at most.
cond-mistake-fixed-4-mmol
Treating 4 mmol/L of lactate as everyone's threshold
Blood lactate at the maximal steady state ranges from about 2 to 8 mmol/L between people, so a fixed 4 mmol/L line misplaces many of them.
cond-table-five-zone-scale
The five-zone intensity scale used in Norwegian endurance sport
Heart rate and lactate ranges per zone, from Seiler and Tønnessen. The authors note the scale ignores differences between people and sports.
cond-vo2max-intervals
VO2 max intervals last 2 to 5 minutes at just above threshold pace
Work bouts of 2 to 5 minutes with equal or shorter rests keep you near peak oxygen uptake. Going harder only cuts the time you can spend there.
cond-interval-blocks-time-course
Plan hard intervals in short blocks on top of an aerobic base
McDonald uses hard intervals for three to six weeks at a time, then returns to base work. Untrained people keep improving for longer.
cond-num-hard-interval-sessions
Ceiling for hard interval sessions
McDonald's upper limit for most people, and for anyone who also lifts or is dieting. Runners rarely tolerate more because of impact.
2 sessions per week
cond-mistake-heart-rate-short-intervals
Pacing short intervals by heart rate
Heart rate needs minutes to catch up with effort, so on a 30-second repeat it reads low. Set short intervals by pace, power or feel.
cond-term-strides
Strides

Short, relaxed accelerations of about 50 to 100 m, or around 20 seconds, at faster than race pace, each followed by a minute or more of rest. Runners do 5 to 10 to practise speed and good form without building fatigue.
cond-beginners-start-easy
Beginners improve on short, easy sessions
Twenty to thirty easy minutes three times a week is enough to start. McDonald builds duration for 4 to 6 weeks before adding intervals.
cond-mistake-running-too-much-too-soon
Running too much, too soon
Novice runners are injured about twice as often per hour as recreational runners. Start with walk-run sessions and build slowly.
cond-num-novice-runner-injuries
Injuries in novice runners
Pooled rate in novice runners, against 7.7 in recreational runners, from a meta-analysis of prospective studies.
17.8 per 1,000 h of running
cond-low-hours-interval-blocks
Very few weekly hours can be met with interval blocks a few times a year
When weekly hours are too low for steady methods to work, an interval-heavy block of about 12 weeks can peak you for an event. It cannot run all year.
cond-mistake-fat-burning-zone
Staying in the 'fat-burning zone' to lose more fat
Easy effort burns a higher share of fat but fewer calories per minute, and fat burned over 24 hours was the same at 40% and 70% of VO2 max.
cond-term-epoc
EPOC (the afterburn)

Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption: the extra oxygen, and so energy, your body uses after a session while it recovers. It rises with intensity and duration, yet stays a small fraction of what the session itself cost.
cond-epoc-is-small
The afterburn adds only a few dozen calories to a session
EPOC is larger after intervals than after steady exercise, but the gap averages about 30 kcal or less. The session itself does the work.
cond-num-epoc-share
EPOC as a share of the session's energy cost
Share of the exercise's net oxygen cost, even after sessions hard or long enough to keep metabolism raised for hours.
6-15 % of session energy
cond-mistake-afterburn-percentage
Picking the workout with the bigger afterburn percentage
A larger percentage of a smaller session can be fewer calories. Longer steady sessions usually burn more in total than short interval sessions.
cond-vigorous-45-minute-afterburn
One chamber study found a larger afterburn after 45 hard minutes
Ten men burned 519 kcal in a hard 45-minute ride and about 190 kcal more over the next 14 hours, while fed enough to stay in energy balance.
cond-intervals-steady-same-fat-loss
Intervals and steady cardio give the same fat loss
Pooled trials find trivial differences in fat mass and lean mass between interval and steady training. Choose by time, recovery and preference.
cond-table-intervals-vs-steady
Intervals versus steady training: what pooled trials found
Findings from meta-analyses and systematic reviews that compared interval training with moderate continuous training.
cond-sprint-intervals-early-gains
A few all-out sprints matched long rides for early fitness gains
In active young men, six sessions of 30-second all-out sprints improved time trials as much as six rides of 90 to 120 minutes.
cond-mistake-tabata-label
Calling any 20-seconds-on, 10-seconds-off circuit a Tabata
The original protocol was 7 to 8 exhaustive bouts at about 170% of VO2 max on a braked bike. Bodyweight circuits do not reach that work rate.
cond-mistake-intervals-plus-heavy-legs
Adding intervals on top of two or three hard leg sessions
Intervals are another hard day for the legs. McDonald's fix is to cut leg lifting to maintenance or to stay with steady cardio.
cond-intervals-on-leg-days
Put intervals on leg-training days, in a separate session if you can
McDonald groups hard leg work on the same days so the legs get two hard days a week instead of four. If both share a session, lift first.
cond-low-carb-and-intervals
Very low carbohydrate intake and frequent hard intervals do not mix
McDonald's rule: the diet sets the training or the training sets the diet. A lot of high-intensity work needs carbohydrate.
cond-dieting-cardio-mix
On a diet, make most cardio steady and keep intervals to one or two sessions
Steady cardio can be done most days without hurting recovery. Intervals cannot, least of all in a deficit with lifting.
cond-term-aerobic-intervals
Aerobic intervals

Easy exercise broken into short bouts with rests, for people who cannot yet keep going for 20 minutes. For example, 5 easy minutes, a short break, then repeat. Over the weeks the bouts get longer and the rests shorter.
cond-beginner-pick-ups
Introduce intensity with short pick-ups inside an easy session
After a month of regular cardio, add 30 to 60 seconds a little faster every 5 minutes. Lengthen the faster parts over several weeks.
cond-early-interval-fat-loss-claims
Early trials that favoured intervals for fat loss did not control diet
The well-known ninefold figure is a skinfold change divided by energy cost. Later pooled trials found no fat-loss advantage for intervals.
cond-fat-loss-three-steps
Stored fat is lost in three steps, and the slow step depends on how lean you are
Fat has to be released from the fat cell, carried away in the blood, then burned. McDonald argues the limiting step differs between lean and obese people.
cond-fasted-cardio-very-lean
Fasted cardio is unproven for very lean dieters, which differs from disproven
The one diet-controlled trial ran 4 weeks in 20 women. McDonald argues it cannot rule out a small benefit in people who are already lean.
cond-mistake-overnight-muscle-glycogen
Thinking a night's sleep empties muscle glycogen
An overnight fast lowers liver glycogen and insulin. Muscle glycogen barely moves, so it does not explain the higher fat use in fasted cardio.
cond-cardio-protein-cost
Cardio burns only a few grams of protein, even with low glycogen
In one small study, protein supplied about 10% of the energy for an hour of cycling when glycogen was depleted, close to 14 g.
cond-mistake-efficiency-excuse
Dropping steady cardio because you 'get efficient' at it
Efficiency changes little and slowly. When a session feels easier you are fitter, so raise the speed, incline or resistance.
cond-term-exercise-efficiency
Exercise efficiency

The share of the energy you burn that becomes external work, with the rest lost as heat. McDonald puts it at about 20 to 25 percent in cycling. Higher efficiency means more speed or power for the same oxygen cost.
cond-num-kilojoules-to-kcal
Energy burned per kilojoule of work on a bike power meter
Rule of thumb from McDonald: at 20 to 25% efficiency the body burns 4 to 5 times the work done, which roughly cancels the 4.2 kJ in a kcal.
about 1 kcal per kJ of work
cond-exercise-small-deficit
Realistic amounts of exercise create a small deficit
At 5 to 10 kcal a minute, burning 500 kcal takes 50 to 100 minutes of exercise. Food intake is usually the easier lever.
cond-mistake-rewarding-workouts
Rewarding a workout with more food than it burned
People often credit a moderate hour with 1,000 kcal when 400 to 500 is nearer the mark, and one snack can cancel a session.
cond-activity-and-weight-maintenance
Keeping weight off is linked with about an hour of activity a day
Successful maintainers report roughly an hour of daily activity, but controlled trials have not shown that exercise prevents regain.
cond-exercise-diet-adherence
Exercise can help you hold a diet, and hunger responses vary
McDonald rates better adherence among the most useful effects of exercise while dieting. Hunger after training differs between people.
cond-real-sprint-training
Real sprint training is a few seconds of work with minutes of rest
Coaches rest sprinters 1 to 2 minutes for every second of maximal sprinting. A proper session takes hours and burns little energy.
cond-mistake-sprinting-unprepared
Running all-out sprints with no preparation
Maximal sprinting is a skill with a real injury cost. Hamstring strains cluster where sprint intensity rises quickly.
cond-mistake-sprinter-physique
Choosing sprints over steady cardio to look like a sprinter
Sport selects body types, and muscular athletes lift. The kind of cardio you do adds little muscle either way.
cond-indoor-blocks
Split long indoor sessions into blocks and change something at each one
Thinking only about the current block makes an hour on a machine easier to finish, and the changes can add useful training.
cond-term-fartlek
Fartlek

Swedish for speed play: an easy session with short, unplanned faster stretches. McDonald suggests a timed version indoors, such as a brief pick-up every few minutes that is quicker than cruising pace without being a sprint.
cond-table-indoor-session-structures
Four ways to structure a steady indoor session
Structures McDonald describes for making indoor cardio pass faster while adding a training effect. The example numbers are illustrations.
cond-term-sports-continuum
Sports continuum

Lyle McDonald's way of placing sports on a line from pure strength and power, through mixed sports such as team and combat sports, to pure endurance. Where a sport sits sets its main training, the adaptations it seeks and its nutrition.
cond-cardio-while-gaining-dose
A little easy cardio fits a gaining phase
McDonald's range while gaining is 20 to 45 minutes, three to five times a week, at or below 70% of maximum heart rate, on low-impact machines.
cond-why-cardio-while-gaining
Why keep some cardio when the goal is muscle
McDonald's reasons: easier recovery, appetite for poor eaters, work capacity for higher-volume lifting, and a smoother start to the next diet.
cond-mistake-zero-to-heavy-cardio
Going from no cardio to a lot of hard cardio when a diet starts
McDonald blames this jump, with a large calorie cut on top, for much of the muscle loss people attribute to cardio.
cond-separate-cardio-from-lifting
Keep cardio and lifting a few hours apart when power matters
Gains in explosive strength were blunted when both were done in one session, less so with 3 hours or more between them.
cond-intervals-lower-body-strength
Intervals alongside lifting slightly reduce lower-body strength gains
Pooled trials found similar muscle growth and upper-body strength with added intervals, but a smaller gain in lower-body strength.
cond-lifting-during-endurance-build
Training for a marathon or century: cut lifting to brief maintenance
Two short full-body sessions a week with the usual loads will hold most strength and size while endurance training takes priority.
cond-lifting-around-long-session
Never lift the day before your long run or ride
McDonald places lifting after the key endurance sessions on the same day, so hard days are grouped and the long session is done fresh.
cond-num-hold-endurance
Sessions a week that held endurance fitness
In general populations endurance was maintained for up to 15 weeks on two sessions a week, or with volume cut 33 to 66%, if intensity stayed the same.
2 sessions per week
cond-unfit-beginner-consistency-first
For a very unfit beginner, the first goal is coming back
McDonald builds the habit before the fitness: short, easy sessions that each end as a small success for the first 3 to 6 weeks.
cond-self-paced-intensity
Let beginners set their own pace, just below where breathing gets hard
Exercise below the ventilatory threshold feels pleasant to most people and exercise above it feels bad, which affects whether they return.
cond-mistake-hard-first-session
Making a beginner's first session as hard as possible
Leaving exhausted and waking up too sore to move teaches a reluctant beginner that exercise is miserable. Many do not return.
cond-very-unfit-cardio-start
Very unfit beginners can start with five minutes of walking
Start from what is manageable, add a minute or two each session, and reach 20 minutes three times a week before raising effort.
cond-num-first-cardio-target
First cardio target for a very unfit beginner
McDonald's first goalpost: continuous, at any pace. Effort is raised only once this has become routine.
20 min, 3 times a week
cond-short-bouts-count
Several short bouts work as well as one long one
Pooled trials found no fitness or blood pressure difference between exercise done in one bout and the same amount split across the day.
cond-mistake-bodyweight-circuits-heavy
Giving a heavy beginner bodyweight circuits
A push-up, burpee or lunge asks someone to move most of a large body weight. Machines and light dumbbells let the load start small.
cond-mistake-lifting-for-metabolism
Filling a heavy beginner's sessions with lifting to 'raise metabolism'
Resting muscle uses about 13 kcal per kg (6 per lb) a day, so added muscle changes daily energy use very little.
cond-strength-and-cardio-day-one
Start strength work and cardio together
McDonald uses a few simple machine exercises from the first session because strength gains show within days, while aerobic gains take weeks to feel.
cond-mistake-testing-first
Opening with calipers and maximum tests
Skinfolds are unreliable and often embarrassing at high body fat, and a maximal test contradicts an easy start. A scale and a tape are enough.
cond-term-metabolic-flexibility
Metabolic flexibility

The ability to switch between burning carbohydrate and burning fat as supply and demand change. McDonald notes it is often reduced with obesity and inactivity, and that regular training helps restore it.
cond-checklist-before-intervals
Before you add hard intervals
Checks drawn from McDonald's articles on interval training. If several fail, stay with steady work for now.
cond-checklist-first-month-unfit
First month for a very unfit beginner
A sequence based on McDonald's approach for heavy, untrained beginners. Each step waits until the one before feels routine.
rec-term-overtraining-syndrome
Overtraining syndrome (OTS)

A performance drop lasting months, usually with fatigue and mood change, after a long stretch in which training and life stress outran recovery. No test confirms it; doctors reach it by excluding other causes.
rec-term-functional-overreaching
Functional overreaching
A short dip in performance after a block of harder training that clears within days to about two weeks of easier work and is followed by performance at or above the earlier level.
rec-term-nonfunctional-overreaching
Non-functional overreaching
A performance drop from more training than recovery allowed that takes weeks to months to clear, often with mood, sleep or hormonal symptoms. Rest restores the old level, but nothing is gained.
rec-table-fatigue-states
From normal tiredness to overtraining syndrome: four states
The states differ mainly in how long performance stays down, which is known only afterwards. Times follow the ECSS and ACSM consensus.
rec-ots-diagnosis-of-exclusion
Overtraining syndrome is diagnosed by ruling other causes out
No blood test or questionnaire confirms overtraining syndrome. A doctor reaches it only after excluding illness, under-eating and other causes.
rec-label-comes-afterwards
Overreaching and overtraining can only be told apart afterwards
The two look alike while they are happening. What separates them is how long recovery takes, so the label arrives after the fact.
rec-mistake-tired-is-not-overtrained
Calling ordinary tiredness overtraining
Feeling flat the day after a hard session is normal training fatigue. Overtraining syndrome means performance stays down for months.
rec-ots-rare-in-lifting
Full overtraining syndrome has barely been documented in lifters
Reviews of resistance training found short-term overreaching and some longer slumps, but minimal evidence of the full syndrome.
rec-num-lifting-overtraining-studies
Lifting studies that tried to overtrain people and saw no drop
In a 2020 systematic review, 10 of the 22 studies that set out to overreach or overtrain lifters found no decline in performance.
10 of 22 studies
rec-planned-overreach-evidence
Driving yourself into a performance dip on purpose is not needed
In trained triathletes, those who came through an overload block merely tired gained more than those pushed into overreaching.
rec-mistake-no-recovery-block
Stretching a hard block and skipping the easy weeks after it
An overload block pays off only when it is short and followed by planned recovery. Extending it turns a useful push into a slump.
rec-mistake-train-harder-in-slump
Answering a slump by training harder
When performance falls for no clear reason, extra work deepens the problem. The usual need is less training and more recovery.
rec-mistake-copying-elite-loads
Copying the training load of elite or full-time athletes
Elite programmes rest on years of gradual build-up and a life arranged around recovery. Taken out of that setting they are too much.
rec-err-on-less
When unsure how much to do, choose the smaller amount
A little less than the ideal amount still brings progress. Too much eventually costs weeks, so the two errors are not equal.
rec-num-young-athletes-nfor
Young athletes who reported a long slump at least once
English athletes of about 15, across 19 sports, who reported non-functional overreaching or overtraining in a survey.
29% of 376 athletes
rec-not-only-training-load
Long slumps are not explained by training load alone
In a survey of 376 young athletes, training load did not predict who reported a long slump. Competitive level and sex did, weakly.
rec-mistake-rotating-muscles
Assuming you cannot overdo it as long as you rotate muscle groups
Fatigue is not only local. Every hard session draws on shared recovery, so splitting the body up does not make unlimited training safe.
rec-recovering-from-slump
Recovery from a long slump is rest, and it cannot be hurried
Reviews give rest or relative rest as the treatment for non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome. Nothing speeds it up.
rec-mistake-dieting-while-recovering
Dieting while trying to recover from a training slump
A calorie deficit is itself a stress and produces many of the same symptoms. Eat at maintenance or slightly above until performance is back.
rec-mistake-same-load-again
Returning to the exact load that caused the slump
If sleep, food and outside stress are unchanged, a load you could not recover from before will fail again.
rec-sustained-drop-only-marker
A sustained drop in performance is the only established marker
For lifting, no blood value, hormone or heart measure has been shown to flag overtraining reliably. Performance that stays down has.
rec-mistake-one-bad-session
Reading one bad session as a sign of overtraining
Single sessions vary for many reasons. A problem shows up as a run of poor sessions over a week or more with no obvious cause.
rec-effort-climbs-first
Rising effort for the same work is an early warning
Before the numbers fall, the same weights or paces start to feel harder. A climbing effort rating at a fixed load deserves attention.
rec-grind-through-risk
Work you can always grind through hides fatigue longest
Near-maximal lifts fail outright when you are run down. Moderate loads can still be finished, so a slow slide goes unnoticed for longer.
rec-overreaching-sleep-illness
Worse sleep and more colds travel with overreaching
In two triathlete studies, only the athletes who became overreached slept less, and they reported far more infections.
rec-num-illness-overreached
Infections reported by overreached triathletes
After 3 weeks of overload, against 22% of athletes who were only tired and 11% of controls, in 27 trained men.
67% of overreached athletes
rec-symptoms-overlap-low-energy
Many overtraining symptoms match those of eating too little
In a 2021 review, 18 of 21 overload studies that tracked intake showed low energy or carbohydrate availability during the hard period.
rec-term-hrv
Heart rate variability (HRV)

The beat-to-beat variation in the time between heartbeats, usually measured on waking and reported as RMSSD. Higher values reflect more parasympathetic (vagal) activity. Read it against your own rolling baseline.
rec-hr-measures-ambiguous
Heart-rate measures move the same way in good adaptation and in overreaching
A 2016 meta-analysis found resting HRV barely changed with overreaching, and other heart-rate measures rose with both fitness and fatigue.
rec-hrv-guided-endurance
Letting daily HRV pick the hard days gave endurance athletes a small edge at most
Two 2021 meta-analyses found HRV-guided endurance training beat a fixed plan on performance by a small margin that was not significant.
rec-hrv-lifting
Timing lifting sessions by HRV did not beat a fixed schedule
In 20 young men, waiting for HRV to return to baseline before each session gave no more strength or muscle than lifting every 48 hours.
rec-resting-hr-method
A morning heart rate helps only if you take it the same way each day
Measure after waking and using the toilet, lying still for several minutes, and compare with your own rested baseline, never with one reading.
rec-num-resting-hr-rule
Rise in morning heart rate that old coaching rules act on
Rule of thumb passed on by McDonald: an easy day at about 5 above your rested norm, a day off at about 10. Crude and untested.
5 and 10 beats per minute
rec-checklist-daily-log
A two-minute daily log for spotting fatigue that is building
Simple self-ratings follow training load better than lab markers. The log shows trends. It cannot diagnose anything.
rec-mood-changes-precede
Mood, sleep and appetite often shift before performance does
Loss of drive, poorer sleep and a dulled appetite tend to appear before the numbers fall, which makes them useful early signals.
rec-warm-up-test
Let the warm-up decide a doubtful session
Feeling flat beforehand predicts little. Do the usual warm-up: if you come good, train as planned, and if you still move badly, stop or go light.
rec-jump-reaction-tests
Jump height and reaction time are optional extra checks, not proven tests
Average jump height tracked fatigue better than best jump in pooled studies. Reaction time is a plausible marker that has not been validated.
rec-term-supercompensation
Supercompensation
The idea that training first lowers a capacity, which then rebounds above its starting level before fading again. It fits muscle glycogen well and describes adaptation in general poorly.
rec-term-fitness-fatigue
Fitness-fatigue model

A two-factor description of training: each session adds both fitness and fatigue, performance reflects fitness minus fatigue, and fatigue fades faster. It is a curve fitted to data, not a biological mechanism.
rec-term-gas
General adaptation syndrome (GAS)
Hans Selye's three-stage account of the response to severe stress: alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Coaches borrowed it to justify periodised training, and how well it fits training is disputed.
rec-no-full-recovery-needed
You do not need to be fully recovered, or better, before training again
In the fitness and fatigue view, sessions overlap. Gains appear over weeks, or once fatigue clears, not as a record at every session.
rec-mistake-break-down-rebuild
Picturing training as breaking muscle down so it rebuilds bigger
Muscle is not smaller after a session and larger after rest. Only glycogen depletes and overshoots, and even that does not stack.
rec-gas-loose-analogy
Selye's stress stages are a loose analogy for training, not a law
Selye's alarm, resistance and exhaustion stages came from rodents given toxic stressors. Researchers disagree on how far they apply to lifting.
rec-table-training-models
Three pictures of how training works, compared
Each model draws a similar curve but leads to different advice. McDonald argues the two-factor model fits practice best. It is still only a description.
rec-one-day-off
Take at least one day a week completely off
McDonald's baseline for everyone from beginner to elite is one day each week with no training, and one or two more that are easy.
rec-term-active-recovery
Active recovery (active rest)
A short, easy session placed between harder days, with less volume and much lower intensity than normal training. McDonald's test is that you leave feeling fresher than you arrived.
rec-term-passive-rest
Passive rest
A day with no training at all. Ordinary walking is allowed. It is the safer choice for anyone who cannot keep an easy session easy.
rec-active-recovery-evidence
Easy sessions reduce soreness a little; a performance benefit is unproven
Pooled trials show active recovery lowers soreness modestly, while the evidence that it improves later performance is weak.
rec-num-active-recovery-volume
Size of a recovery session against a normal one
McDonald's guide: half to two thirds of usual volume, at about 60% of maximum heart rate, or at most 75% of 1RM for easy sets of 3 to 5.
50-67% of normal volume
rec-mistake-recovery-becomes-workout
Turning a recovery session into a workout
An easy day that creeps up in load or length adds fatigue, blunts the next hard day and leaves every session at the same middling effort.
rec-recovery-day-technique
A light day can double as technique practice if you are fresh enough to move well
Low loads let you rehearse a lift without fatigue. If you are too tired to move well, do something simple that needs no skill.
rec-table-planned-rest
Planned rest at four time scales
Rest is scheduled weekly, inside each block, between blocks and yearly. The intervals are McDonald's coaching guides and survey habits, not trial results.
rec-hard-days-limit
Keep truly hard sessions for the same lift or muscle to one or two a week
Most athletes manage two or three truly hard days a week. Lifters can train hard more often only because the lifts and muscles rotate.
rec-mistake-same-effort-always
Training at the same effort every day, all year
When easy days are pushed and hard days suffer for it, the week settles at medium effort, and without easier weeks progress stalls.
rec-term-hlm
Heavy-light-medium training
A weekly pattern for training the same lifts three times: one heavy day, one light day and one in between. Bill Starr popularised it for lifters who had grown too strong to go heavy at every session.
rec-hlm-loads
Set the light and medium days as a share of the heavy day's weight
A common setting is 65 to 75 percent of the heavy day's load on the light day and 75 to 85 percent on the medium day, for the same reps.
rec-hlm-ways-to-lighten
A day can be made lighter by load, by reps in reserve or by exercise choice
Lower the weight on the same lift, change the rep range while staying short of failure, or swap to a variation that limits the load.
rec-mistake-light-day-to-failure
Taking the light and medium days to failure
A lighter weight taken to a rep maximum is still a maximal effort. Three such days a week leave no easy day at all.
rec-failure-slows-recovery
Sets taken to failure take a day or two longer to recover from
In ten trained men, three sets of ten to failure slowed recovery for 24 to 48 hours compared with the same reps done as six sets of five.
rec-term-two-a-day
Two-a-day training

Two separate sessions in one day with a real break between them. In this guide it means working the same lifts or muscles in both, as distinct from a split that puts different body parts in the morning and the evening.
rec-two-a-day-evidence
Splitting the same work into two daily sessions has shown little extra benefit so far
In weightlifters and trained men, twice-daily sessions matched once-daily sessions for muscle size, with a strength edge in some measures only.
rec-two-a-day-reasons
The case for two sessions a day is quality, practice and scheduling
Shorter sessions hold intensity better, allow more fresh practice of technical lifts, and can free whole rest days when doubled.
rec-mistake-two-full-sessions
Doing two full workouts from the first day of twice-daily training
Doubling the work at once is the usual way this fails. Start by splitting what you already do, at about 40 to 45 minutes a session.
rec-two-a-day-heavy-light
Make one of the two sessions heavy and the other light
McDonald's view is that almost nobody benefits from two truly heavy sessions in a day, at the start or later.
rec-num-two-a-day-gap
Break between two sessions on the same day
A rule of thumb with no trial behind it: time for a meal or two and a rest. McDonald treats 3.5 to 7 hours as fine. A review lists over 6 hours among preventive measures.
4-6 hours
rec-six-days-setup
Six short lifting days work when volume is spread and effort is held back
With weekly volume and load equal, six sessions a week gave trained men the same gains as three, so the choice is about schedule.
rec-mistake-six-day-shoulders
Arranging a six-day split so the shoulders work hard four days a week
Three-way splits run twice a week load the shoulder joint on four days. An upper and lower rotation cuts that to three.
rec-term-doms
Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)
Muscle tenderness and stiffness that builds in the day or two after unaccustomed or eccentric-heavy exercise and fades over several days. It is most common early in a programme and after a layoff.
rec-term-repeated-bout
Repeated bout effect

The protection that one session of unaccustomed eccentric exercise gives against damage and soreness from later sessions. It is why soreness fades within a few sessions even when the work stays the same.
rec-soreness-and-frequency
Training a muscle more often brings less soreness, not less growth
In McDonald's experience, lifters who train each muscle two or three times a week report far less soreness than once-a-week trainers and grow at least as well.
rec-training-while-sore
Training a sore muscle again did not worsen damage in a controlled trial
In 51 athletes, repeating hard eccentric arm work three days after the first bout neither added damage nor slowed recovery.
rec-mistake-soreness-as-readiness
Using soreness to decide whether a muscle has recovered
Soreness tracks damage and strength loss poorly. No soreness does not prove a muscle is recovered, and soreness does not prove it is not.
rec-severe-soreness-warning
Extreme pain after a punishing new session can be a medical emergency
Exertional rhabdomyolysis is rare but can be life-threatening. Dark urine after very hard unaccustomed exercise needs immediate medical care.
rec-term-detraining
Detraining
The partial or complete loss of training adaptations when training stops or falls too low. Strength, power and muscle size fall at different rates, and the losses grow with the length of the break.
rec-term-muscle-memory
Muscle memory

The observation that lost strength and muscle return faster than they were first built. Proposed explanations are retained nuclei in muscle fibres, lasting epigenetic changes and retained skill. None is settled in humans.
rec-short-break-costs-little
A few days off costs almost nothing, and some lifters come back stronger
Three to five days without training left lower-body strength intact in trained lifters, and two weeks off did not lower leg press strength in trained men.
rec-detraining-dose
Strength loss grows with time off and is larger in older and inactive people
A meta-analysis of 103 studies found stopping training lowered submaximal strength most, maximal force next and power least, in step with time off.
rec-breaks-no-long-term-cost
Breaks of a few weeks did not reduce long-term gains in beginners
In two trials, people who stopped for 3 or 10 weeks and then resumed ended with the same strength and muscle size as people who trained straight through.
rec-muscle-memory-evidence
Regaining is faster than gaining; why is still argued over
Retraining restores lost size and strength quickly. Whether retained muscle nuclei explain it is disputed in human studies.
rec-num-return-ratio
Time to get back after one to two weeks off
McDonald's rule of thumb: two weeks off takes about four weeks to regain. It stops applying once the break reaches a month or more.
2x the time off
rec-mistake-restart-old-weights
Restarting at your old weights after months away
Loads from before a long layoff are the quickest route to an injury, or to soreness bad enough to stop you coming back.
rec-return-after-long-layoff
After months off, restart as a beginner and expect to move faster than one
McDonald's plan: one light set of each exercise, whole body, at half to 60 percent of old loads, adding a little every few sessions.
rec-num-return-starting-load
Starting load after a long layoff
McDonald's starting point, or lighter, for the first sessions back after months away, for one or two easy sets per exercise.
50-60% of previous max
rec-table-return-by-break
Coming back after a break: what to expect by time away
Losses grow with time away and return faster than they were built. The restart advice is McDonald's; the losses are from trials.
rec-injury-return-rules
After an injury, wait a week longer than you think and test one exercise at a time
McDonald's two rules: when it feels healed, give it another week, then bring back one set of one exercise at a time.
rec-maintenance-dose
When time is short, a small dose holds most of your strength
A review found younger adults kept strength and size for up to 32 weeks on one session a week and one set per exercise, if loads stayed heavy.
rec-life-stress-slows-gains
High life stress slowed strength gains and recovery in students
In two student studies, people under more life stress gained less strength in 12 weeks and regained force more slowly after a hard leg session.
rec-num-exam-week-injury
Injury restrictions in exam weeks against ordinary weeks
Odds of a player having an injury restriction in weeks of high academic stress, in 101 college football players over a season.
1.78 odds ratio
rec-term-allostatic-load
Allostatic load
The cumulative cost to the body of adapting to every stressor it meets. Training, work, short sleep, dieting and emotional strain draw on the same stress response, so they add together.
rec-term-under-recovery
Under-recovery
A name some prefer to overtraining. It places the fault in too little sleep, food or rest to absorb the training, and not in the training itself, which may be what the goal requires.
rec-improve-recovery-before-cutting
When training cannot come down further, raise recovery
Every goal needs some minimum amount of training. Once you are near that floor, the lever left is recovery: sleep, food and less outside stress.
rec-term-dietary-restraint
Cognitive dietary restraint
The ongoing, deliberate effort to limit eating in order to control body weight, measured by questionnaire. It describes a mindset and does not always mean eating less.
rec-restraint-cortisol
Women who restricted eating most strictly excreted more cortisol
In two cross-sectional studies, women with high dietary restraint scores had higher 24-hour urinary cortisol than women with low scores.
rec-dieting-is-a-stress
A calorie deficit counts as stress and lowers what you can recover from
Calorie restriction raised cortisol in controlled studies, mostly with severe restriction and early on, and deficits blunt what training builds.
rec-mistake-deficit-plus-volume
Pairing a steep calorie deficit with large amounts of hard exercise
McDonald's rule is to cut calories hard or do a lot of activity, not both. The pairing often stalls and wears people down.
nut-energy-balance-slow
Body weight follows energy balance, but it moves slowly
Eat above what you burn and weight rises, eat below and it falls, but the change takes months to show its full size.
nut-maintenance-is-an-estimate
Calorie calculators give a starting point, not your maintenance
Even the best resting-rate equation is within 10 percent of measured for most people, and many individuals fall outside it.
nut-protein-range
Most lifters do well on 1.6 to 2.2 g of protein per kg a day
About 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg (0.7 to 1.0 g per lb) of body weight a day covers most people who lift to build muscle.
nut-protein-kidneys
High protein does not harm kidney function in healthy adults
In healthy adults without kidney disease, higher protein intakes did not reduce kidney filtration in trials.
nut-protein-per-meal
Spread protein over several meals, but the split matters less than the total
About 0.25 to 0.55 g per kg per meal is a sound target (20 to 40 g for most people), and the daily total is what matters most.
nut-protein-timing-window
Protein timing around training matters little next to the daily total
Eating protein straight after training is fine, but a precise window does not change results once daily intake is met.
nut-protein-plant-animal
Plant protein builds muscle about as well, given enough total protein
When total protein is adequate, plant and animal sources give similar muscle and strength gains over months.
nut-carbs-for-lifting
Carbohydrate boosts lifting only in long, high-volume sessions
Carbohydrate intake had little effect on strength training in short fed sessions, and may help when volume is high.
nut-fat-minimum
Keep fat from falling too low: about 15 to 30 percent of calories
Fat of roughly 0.5 to 1.5 g per kg, or 15 to 30 percent of energy, is a sound band, and very low fat has costs.
nut-fibre-target
Aim for 25 to 29 g of fibre a day
In large analyses, health benefits from fibre were greatest at about 25 to 29 g a day, with more possibly better.
nut-meal-timing-training
Pre-workout eating helps in long sessions, and little else about timing is critical
Daily totals decide results, and a meal before training mostly helps if you train fasted or do high volume.
nut-hydration-performance
Being under-hydrated lowers strength and muscle endurance
Hypohydration reduced strength by about 5.5 percent and muscle endurance by about 8 percent in a meta-analysis.
nut-alcohol-recovery
Heavy drinking after hard training blunts the muscle repair signal
A very large dose of alcohol after training cut muscle protein synthesis by 24 to 37 percent in one small study.
nut-alcohol-energy
Alcohol adds calories that people do not offset by eating less
Across 22 studies, people did not eat less after drinking, so total energy for the day rose.
nut-creatine
Creatine monohydrate is the best-supported lifting supplement
Taking 3 to 5 g of creatine monohydrate a day adds lean mass when combined with training, and it is safe for healthy people.
nut-caffeine
Caffeine gives a small, real boost to strength and power
In a meta-analysis, caffeine raised maximal strength and power slightly, mostly in the upper body.
nut-beta-alanine-citrulline
Beta-alanine and citrulline help in specific cases, with modest effects
Beta-alanine helps efforts of one to four minutes, and citrulline malate added about three reps per exercise.
nut-supplement-skepticism
Most supplements lack good evidence, and some carry risks
The IOC finds only a few supplements, including caffeine and creatine, have good evidence, and the rest are unproven.
nut-logging-helps
Logging food is linked to better results, and frequency matters most
People who logged more often lost more, and a rough log kept consistently beats a perfect one kept rarely.
nut-label-tolerance
US labels may legally run up to 20 percent above the declared calories
A US food is misbranded only if its calories exceed the declared value by more than 20 percent.
nut-under-reporting
Under-reporting is the norm, even among athletes and dietitians
Self-reported intake is usually below true intake, by around a fifth in athletes and by more in some groups.
nut-tracking-risk
Tracking can feed disordered eating in people who are prone to it
Calorie apps are linked to more eating-disorder symptoms in surveys, and many patients blame them.
nut-hand-portions
Hand portions are a rougher but gentler way to estimate food
Using your hand as a ruler reached within 25 percent of the true weight for most simple foods in one study.
nut-mistake-raw-cooked
Weighing cooked food but logging the raw entry
Raw and cooked weights differ by the water gained or lost, so the entry must match the state you weighed.
nut-mistake-cooking-oil
Forgetting cooking oil and butter
Fat has 9 kcal per gram, so a splash of oil in the pan can add a few hundred calories unseen.
nut-mistake-eyeballing
Eyeballing dense foods like nut butter, cheese and cereal
Eyeballed portions of calorie-dense foods are easy to get wrong, and small errors there cost the most calories.
nut-mistake-database-entry
Taking the first database entry without checking it
App databases are good on average but hold wrong and duplicate entries that can swing a meal by hundreds of calories.
nut-mistake-bites-drinks
Not logging drinks, bites, tastes and sauces
Small unlogged items are a large part of why logs read low.
nut-mistake-restaurant-menu
Logging a restaurant meal at the number on the menu
Restaurant meals often hold more energy than stated, and the error is largest on individual items.
nut-mistake-weekends
Tracking weekdays carefully and weekends loosely
Weekend eating and activity can erase much of a weekday deficit.
nut-mistake-all-or-nothing
Treating the tracker as exact, or quitting after one bad day
Tracker numbers are estimates with real error, and a single high day changes little.
nut-num-protein-range
Daily protein for lifters
The common target for building muscle: 0.7 to 1.0 g per lb a day.
1.6-2.2 g per kg per day
nut-num-protein-meal
Protein per serving
ISSN guide: 0.25 g per kg, or 20 to 40 g, a serving. A bodybuilding review suggests 0.40 to 0.55 g per kg per meal.
0.25-0.55 g per kg per meal
nut-num-atwater
Energy per gram of food
Protein 4, carbohydrate 4, fat 9 and alcohol 7 kcal per gram on food labels.
4 · 4 · 9 · 7 kcal per g
nut-num-equation-error
Accuracy of the best equation
Mifflin-St Jeor was within 10 percent of measured resting rate for the most people.
10 % error band
nut-num-activity-range
Activity multiplier range
Long-term sustainable activity levels for free-living adults, per FAO/WHO/UNU.
1.40-2.40 times resting rate
nut-num-label-slack
US label tolerance
A food is misbranded only above this; a typical snack runs a few percent over.
+20 % over the label
nut-num-underreport
Under-reporting in athletes
Self-reported energy intake was this much lower than measured expenditure.
19 % of true intake
nut-num-creatine
Creatine monohydrate dose
Daily dose from a physique-athlete review; lean-mass gain was about 1.1 kg with training.
3-5 g per day
nut-num-caffeine
Caffeine dose often studied
ISSN 2010: about 3 to 6 mg per kg works, 9 or more adds nothing; 5 mg/kg is 2.3 mg per lb. Half-life was 7.9 h on low-dose oral contraceptives, 5.4 h without.
3-6 mg per kg
nut-num-fibre
Fibre target
Intake at which health benefits were greatest in pooled studies.
25-29 g per day
nut-term-maintenance
Maintenance calories
The daily energy intake at which your body weight stays steady over weeks. Also called total daily energy expenditure.
nut-term-rmr
Resting metabolic rate (RMR)
The energy your body uses at rest to keep you alive, usually 60 to 70 percent of a day for inactive people, estimated by equations or measured.
nut-term-tef
Thermic effect of food (TEF)
The energy used to digest, absorb and store food, about 5 to 15 percent of daily energy expenditure on a mixed diet, and higher with protein and alcohol.
nut-term-atwater
Atwater factors
Standard energy values per gram that food labels use: 4 kcal for protein and carbohydrate, 9 for fat, 7 for alcohol. They are averages, not measurements of your food.
nut-term-macronutrients
Macronutrients (macros)
The three nutrients that provide most energy: protein, carbohydrate and fat. Alcohol is sometimes counted as a fourth source of energy.
nut-term-leucine
Leucine
An essential amino acid that acts as a trigger for muscle protein synthesis. Animal proteins contain more than most plant proteins, per gram of protein.
nut-term-kilojoule
Kilojoule (kJ) and kilocalorie (kcal)
Two units of food energy. One kcal, the calorie on most labels, equals 4.184 kJ. Many countries print kJ.
nut-term-ergogenic
Ergogenic aid
Something taken to improve exercise performance or training results. Creatine and caffeine are the best-supported examples.
nut-table-protein-targets
Protein targets by goal and body weight
Daily protein in g per kg and per lb, with worked examples for 70 kg (154 lb) and 90 kg (198 lb) people.
nut-table-hand-portions
Hand-portion guide
A rough guide for estimating a serving with your own hand when you do not weigh food. Check it against a scale once.
nut-table-supplements
Supplement evidence at a glance
How the common supplements rate for people who lift, from strongest to weakest evidence.
nut-term-essential-nutrient
Essential, nonessential and conditionally essential nutrients

Essential: needed and not made in enough amount, so food must supply it. Nonessential: needed, but the body builds its own. Conditionally essential: supply falls short only in some states; McDonald puts carbohydrate there for hard training.
nut-term-essential-fatty-acids
Essential fatty acids (EFAs)

Fats the body needs but cannot build: by the textbook, linoleic acid (LA, omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, omega-3). McDonald's view is that almost any diet with fat covers the minimum, not the optimum. See the diet planner.
nut-ala-conversion
Plant omega-3 (ALA) converted poorly to DHA in tracer studies, least in men
In tracer studies, young men made some EPA from ALA but no measurable DHA, while young women converted about 21 percent to EPA and 9 percent to DHA.
nut-efa-aa-dha
McDonald argues arachidonic acid and DHA may be the real essential fats
LA and ALA are the textbook essential fats, but much of what they do runs through their products. McDonald's reading is that arachidonic acid (AA) and DHA are the ones the body truly needs.
nut-mistake-linoleic-fear
Cutting vegetable oils for fear that omega-6 fat inflames the body
In 15 randomised trials of healthy people, adding linoleic acid, the main omega-6 fat, did not raise blood markers of inflammation.
nut-trans-fat
Keep industrial trans fat as close to zero as you can
Trans fat from partially hydrogenated oils harms blood lipids, and intakes of about 2 percent of energy went with a markedly higher rate of heart disease.
nut-lactose-dose
Most adults with lactose intolerance tolerated about a cup of milk's lactose
In a systematic review, 12 to 15 g of lactose, roughly one cup of milk, was well tolerated by most adults with lactose intolerance or malabsorption.
nut-num-fibre-energy
Energy from dietary fibre
FAO factor for fibre in ordinary foods, from gut bacteria fermenting part of it. Fibre they cannot ferment gives none.
2 kcal per g (8 kJ)
nut-protein-net-energy
On a proposed net energy scale, protein counts for less than its label value
Labels count protein at 4 kcal (17 kJ) per gram. On a net energy scale the FAO describes but has not adopted, it is worth 3.2 kcal (13 kJ).
nut-mps-not-whole-story
McDonald argues per-meal protein caps ignore breakdown and non-muscle tissue
In young adults, a meal with about 70 g of protein gave better whole-body protein balance than one with 40 g, mostly by cutting protein breakdown.
nut-connective-tissue-turnover
In six knee-surgery patients, tendon and cartilage made protein at rates near muscle's
In six patients having knee replacement, basal protein synthesis in tendon, ligament, cartilage and menisci did not differ significantly from muscle.
nut-mcdonald-protein-targets
McDonald sets lifters at 2.2 g per kg of protein, and high-level athletes higher
McDonald's practice: about 2.2 g per kg (1 g per lb) for recreational lifters outside a diet, and 2.5 to 3.0 g per kg (1.1 to 1.4 g per lb) for high-level strength athletes.
nut-protein-bone
Higher protein did not harm bone, and may help the spine slightly
A meta-analysis of 16 trials and 20 cohort studies found no harm to bone from higher protein, and a possible small gain in lumbar spine density.
nut-table-amino-acids
Essential amino acids and leucine in common protein powders
Share of the protein in each isolate, measured in one lab. A dash means the figure was not in the summary. Plant isolates vary widely, and blends of them can come close to animal profiles.
nut-term-pdcaas
PDCAAS (protein digestibility-corrected amino acid score)

A protein quality score adopted by FAO/WHO in 1991. It compares a protein's essential amino acids with a reference pattern for young children, corrects for digestibility over the whole gut, and is capped at 1.0, so top proteins tie.
nut-term-diaas
DIAAS (digestible indispensable amino acid score)

The score FAO has recommended in place of PDCAAS. It uses the digestibility of each essential amino acid at the end of the small intestine and is not capped. In rats it ran from 0.01 for a corn cereal to 1.18 for milk protein concentrate.
nut-mistake-quality-scores
Ranking protein sources by quality score when you already eat plenty
McDonald's view is that quality scores matter most for diets short of protein, and that at a lifter's intake from mixed sources, gaps between good proteins matter little.
nut-term-fast-slow-protein
Fast and slow proteins

Proteins whose amino acids reach the blood at different speeds. Whey gives a sharp, short rise in blood amino acids; casein gives a lower rise that lasts for hours, probably because it leaves the stomach slowly.
nut-whey-casein-context
Whey and casein differ most when eaten alone, less in a mixed meal
In a single-protein meal, casein left more protein in the body over 7 hours than whey did. Early results suggest added carbohydrate and fat narrow the gap.
nut-protein-40g-whole-body
After whole-body training, 40 g of whey beat 20 g for muscle protein synthesis
In 30 resistance-trained young men, 40 g of whey after a whole-body session raised muscle protein synthesis about 20 percent more than 20 g, whatever their lean mass.
nut-mistake-raw-eggs
Eating eggs raw for their protein
In five people with an ileostomy, about 51 percent of raw egg protein was absorbed by the end of the small intestine, against 91 percent when cooked.
nut-plant-b12-iron
Without animal foods, plan for vitamin B12, and expect less iron to be absorbed
B12 depletion was common among vegetarians, more so vegans. In people with no iron stores, about 5 to 12 percent of iron is absorbed from vegetarian diets, 14 to 18 from mixed.
nut-term-fibre-types
Soluble, insoluble and fermentable fibre

Soluble (viscous) fibre forms a gel in water and slows stomach emptying. Insoluble fibre does not dissolve and adds bulk. Fermentable fibre is broken down by gut bacteria into gases and short-chain fatty acids, which supply some energy.
nut-fibre-big-eaters
McDonald warns that high fibre can work against big eaters
More fibre lowered how much fat and protein the gut absorbed in a feeding study. McDonald's view is that this and the fullness help dieters and hinder big eaters.
nut-term-glycaemic-load
Glycaemic load (GL)

A food's glycaemic index multiplied by the grams of carbohydrate in the portion eaten, divided by 100. It accounts for both the kind and the amount of carbohydrate (see the glycaemic index entry in the diet guide).
nut-mistake-gi-portion
Ruling out a food for its glycaemic index without looking at the portion
GI is measured on a serving that holds 50 g of available carbohydrate, so a high value says little about a vegetable eaten in small amounts.
nut-gi-not-insulin
A lower glycaemic index does not always mean less insulin
In six healthy men, a low-GI bran cereal raised insulin sooner than high-GI corn flakes. Its lower GI came from faster glucose removal, not slower entry.
nut-gi-training-state
The same cereal scored a different glycaemic index in trained and sedentary men
One breakfast cereal's GI differed by about 23 units between endurance-trained and sedentary young men, so a published value may not fit everyone.
nut-low-gl-weight-loss
Lowering glycaemic index or load added nothing to a calorie deficit in a feeding trial
In 29 adults with obesity on provided food for 12 weeks, high-GI, low-GI and high-fat diets with the same deficit lost similar weight.
nut-glycogen-refuel-speed
Carbohydrate eaten straight after hard exercise refills glycogen fastest
After depleting exercise, glycogen refilled fastest with carbohydrate taken at once, and a delay of hours could halve the rate. McDonald thinks this matters mainly for same-day sessions.
nut-carb-load-who
Carbohydrate loading helps in endurance events of more than about 90 minutes
Raising muscle glycogen above normal delayed fatigue by about 20 percent in events over 90 minutes, and did not help efforts under 5 minutes or runs and rides of 60 to 90.
nut-carb-load-one-day
A short all-out effort and one day of high carbohydrate loaded glycogen in a small study
In seven endurance-trained athletes, 3 minutes of very hard cycling then 24 hours at about 10 g/kg of high-GI carbohydrate nearly doubled muscle glycogen.
nut-bodybuilder-carb-load
Bodybuilders who carb-loaded before a show measured bigger, and many had diarrhoea
After three low-carbohydrate days, 15 male bodybuilders who loaded for 24 hours gained muscle thickness and photo scores; 9 who did not load had no change in thickness or girths.
nut-mistake-overdrinking-race
Drinking more than you sweat out during a long race
In the 2002 Boston Marathon, 13 percent of 488 sampled runners finished with low blood sodium; weight gain during the race and finishing after 4 hours went with it.
nut-liquid-calories
Calories from sugary drinks were not offset by eating less
In a crossover trial, 450 kcal a day of jelly beans was matched by eating less, while the same calories as soda were simply added on and weight rose.
nut-milk-recovery-drink
Milk did well as a drink after sweaty endurance sessions in small trials
Low-fat milk was retained better than water or a sports drink after sweating, and chocolate milk beat a matched carbohydrate drink between two cycling bouts.
nut-term-energy-density
Energy density

Calories per gram of food. Water, fibre and air lower it; fat raises it, and so does removing water. Refined low-fat foods can still be energy dense. Low values help dieters feel full, and high values help people who must eat a lot.
nut-soy-thyroid
Soy did not upset thyroid hormones in healthy adults with enough iodine
Across 18 randomised trials, soy did not change thyroid hormones and nudged TSH up very slightly. People treated for an underactive thyroid are a separate case.
nut-soy-testosterone
Soy protein and isoflavones did not change men's testosterone
A meta-analysis of 41 studies found no effect of soy foods, soy protein or isoflavone extracts on testosterone or oestrogen in men, at any dose or duration tested.
nut-term-isoflavones
Isoflavones (soy phytoestrogens)

Plant compounds in soy, chiefly genistein and daidzein, that bind oestrogen receptors and can act like oestrogen. Phytoestrogen is the wider term for such plant compounds. They drive most worries about soy and hormones.
nut-hfcs-like-sugar
High-fructose corn syrup behaves much like table sugar
HFCS and sucrose are both mixes of fructose and glucose, and in 34 adults they gave similar 24-hour glucose, insulin, leptin and blood fat profiles.
nut-num-fructose-50g
Fructose intake below which blood fats did not rise after meals
In pooled trials of pure fructose, under 50 g a day had no clear effect on blood fats after meals, and fasting levels and body weight held up to 100 g.
50 g of fructose a day
nut-fish-mercury
Choose lower-mercury fish, above all in pregnancy and for children
US FDA and EPA advice lists seven fish to avoid for their mercury, such as swordfish, shark and orange roughy, and many low-mercury picks such as salmon and sardines.
nut-antioxidants-adaptation
High-dose vitamins C and E blunted some training adaptations in trials
In two randomised trials, daily vitamin C and E dulled muscle markers of adaptation, though fitness and muscle growth mostly kept pace with placebo.
nut-mistake-antioxidant-pills
Taking antioxidant pills as health insurance
In 78 randomised trials with 296,707 people, antioxidant pills did not lower deaths, and beta-carotene and vitamin E slightly raised them in the better trials.
nut-vitamin-d-athletes
Many athletes test low in vitamin D, but the count depends on the cut-off
At a cut-off of 32 ng/mL, 56 percent of 2,313 athletes were low, more in winter and in indoor sports. The IOM counts 20 ng/mL as enough for nearly everyone.
nut-glutamine
Glutamine added no strength or lean mass in a training trial
In 31 young adults lifting for six weeks, a large daily glutamine dose did no better than placebo for strength, lean mass or muscle breakdown.
nut-muscle-full
Muscle protein synthesis rose and fell back within hours of a protein dose
After 48 g of whey, synthesis in eight young men peaked at 45 to 90 minutes and returned to baseline while blood amino acids were still high.
nut-presleep-protein
Protein before bed improved overnight protein balance after evening training
In 16 young men who lifted in the evening, 40 g of casein 30 minutes before sleep was digested overnight and improved whole-body protein balance.
nut-surplus-elite-athletes
A planned surplus added fat but no extra lean mass in young elite athletes
Over 8 to 12 weeks of added strength work, elite athletes given a surplus meal plan gained more weight and fat than those eating freely, and similar lean mass.
nut-term-ketosis
Ketosis and ketone bodies

Ketone bodies are fuels the liver makes from fat when carbohydrate is scarce; ketosis means raised blood ketones and follows fat breakdown. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a separate danger: with diabetes, see a clinician before going low-carb.
nut-mistake-ketone-strips
Judging a low-carbohydrate diet by urine ketone strips
Strips detect ketones spilling into urine, not blood levels or fat loss. McDonald's view is that they can read negative during ketosis and that fat lost is what counts.
diet-deficit-rule-of-thumb
The 3,500 kcal per pound rule is a rough guide that varies with body fat
About 3,500 kcal (7,700 per kg) per pound of loss is only an average, and leaner people need less per unit lost.
diet-deficit-rate
Aim to lose about 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week
A pace of 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week is the usual advice for keeping muscle while getting leaner.
diet-deficit-muscle-cost
Deficits much beyond 500 kcal a day cost lean mass in lifters
In a meta-regression, a deficit of about 500 kcal a day stopped lean-mass gains from training, while strength held up.
diet-mistake-too-fast
Losing over 1 percent of body weight a week without high protein and heavy lifting
Bigger deficits take a larger share of the loss from lean mass, and athletes who lost more slowly gained lean mass. Going faster needs high protein and heavy lifting.
diet-num-rate
Rate of loss
Usual pace for keeping muscle; at 80 kg (176 lb) that is 0.4 to 0.8 kg a week.
0.5-1 % body weight per week
diet-num-deficit-limit
Deficit that stopped lean-mass gains
In a meta-regression, deficits around this size prevented gains in lean mass in people doing resistance training.
500 kcal per day
diet-num-3500
